articles.title: Acidente em BH: Motorista com sinais de embriaguez bate em árvore | G1
articles.standfirst: Homem de aproximadamente 50 anos ficou ferido e precisou ser retirado pelo porta-malas do veículo. Segundo os bombeiros, havia várias latas de cerveja dentro do carro.
articles.summary: Acidente em BH na Avenida Carlos Luz deixou motorista ferido após batida em árvore; bombeiros encontraram latas de cerveja no carro durante o resgate da vítima.
articles.body:
Carro bateu em árvore na Avenida Presidente Carlos Luz, em Belo Horizonte, durante forte chuva neste domingo — Foto: CBMMG/Reprodução

Um motorista de aproximadamente 50 anos ficou ferido após perder o controle do carro e bater em uma árvore na Avenida Presidente Carlos Luz , próximo à Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (UFMG), em Belo Horizonte, na tarde deste domingo (1º). Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros , o homem apresentava sinais de embriaguez.

O acidente aconteceu por volta das 12h15, na altura do número 1001 da avenida, durante uma forte pancada de chuva na região. O motorista dirigia um Volkswagen Gol no sentido Centro quando, conforme relatou aos militares, perdeu o controle da direção e atingiu a árvore.

Com o impacto, o condutor ficou retido dentro do veículo e se queixava de fortes dores na região da pelve e nas pernas. Três viaturas do Corpo de Bombeiros foram mobilizadas para atender à ocorrência.

Os militares estabilizaram o carro, desconectaram os cabos da bateria e retiraram o homem pelo porta-malas. Ele estava consciente, mas apresentava suspeita de fraturas na pelve e na perna direita. Em seguida, foi encaminhado aos cuidados de uma equipe do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) .

Durante o atendimento, os bombeiros perceberam sinais de possível embriaguez no motorista. Dentro do veículo, foram encontradas várias latas de cerveja, algumas vazias e outras ainda fechadas.

Até o momento, não há informações sobre a realização de teste do bafômetro ou a confirmação de ingestão de bebida alcoólica pelo condutor.

articles.title: Lavrador é preso suspeito de matar a namorada a facadas em Prudente | G1
articles.standfirst: Benilto José dos Santos foi encontrado com uma faca na mão e roupas sujas de sangue no sábado (31); ele admitiu ter golpeado Maria Rosa Zanardo, mas alegou legítima defesa.
articles.summary: Preso por feminicídio em Presidente Prudente, lavrador de 66 anos confessou ter matado a namorada após discussão motivada por ciúmes e consumo de álcool no sábado.
articles.body:
Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher (DDM) de Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Beatriz Jarins/g1

Um lavrador de 66 anos foi preso, no sábado (31), em Presidente Prudente (SP) suspeito de matar a namorada, de 70 anos, a facadas. Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, os policiais encontraram a Maria Rosa Zanardo caída próximo à porta da sala.

O caso ocorreu no bairro Jardim Humberto Salvador e foi registrado como feminicídio na Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher (DDM). De acordo com o registro policial, o suspeito do crime, Benilto José dos Santos, estava no banheiro do imóvel e tinha as roupas sujas de sangue.

Ao chegar ao endereço, os policiais encontraram os vizinhos exaltadas do lado de fora, ameaçando o homem. A porta do apartamento precisou ser arrombada. Quando entrou, a equipe encontrou Benilto com uma faca na mão.

No interrogatório, o homem admitiu ter atingido a mulher com golpes de faca, mas alegou que agiu em legítima defesa. Ele afirmou que havia ingerido vodca e que a discussão começou por ciúmes, porque suspeitava que a vítima estivesse com outro homem.

Segundo a versão apresentada por ele, Maria Rosa teria pegado uma faca e avançado contra ele, cortando um de seus dedos. Os celulares da vítima e do suspeito foram apreendidos.

Benilto foi preso em flagrante por feminicídio , com agravante pelo fato de o crime ter sido cometido contra uma pessoa com mais de 60 anos.

articles.title: Presidente do TJMS assume governo após afastamento de Riedel | G1
articles.standfirst: Dorival Renato Pavan assume o comando do estado a partir deste domingo (1º), devido à ausência do governador, do vice-governador e do presidente da Assembleia Legislativa.
articles.summary: Dorival Renato Pavan assume o comando do estado a partir deste domingo (1º), devido à ausência do governador, do vice-governador e do presidente da Assembleia Legislativa.
articles.body:
Eduardo Riedel (PP) sai de licença e Des. Dorival Renato Pavan assume chefia do Governo de MS até 6 de novembro de 2026 — Foto: Saul Schramm/GOV-MS // OAB-MS

O presidente do Tribunal de Justiça de Mato Grosso do Sul (TJMS), desembargador Dorival Renato Pavan, assume o governo do estado neste domingo (1º) e permanece no cargo até sexta-feira (6). A mudança ocorre porque o governador Eduardo Riedel (PP), o vice-governador José Carlos Barbosa, o Barbosinha (Republicanos), e o presidente da Assembleia Legislativa, Gerson Claro (PP), estarão afastados das funções nesse período.

Riedel comunicou o afastamento em um ofício enviado à Assembleia Legislativa de Mato Grosso do Sul (Alems). No documento, informou que ficará licenciado do cargo entre 1º e 6 de novembro e que poderá viajar para fora do estado ou do país.

O documento também informa que Barbosinha, primeiro na linha sucessória, estará afastado das funções no mesmo período.

A assessoria do Governo do Estado não informou o motivo do afastamento de Riedel e Barbosinha.

Com a ausência dos dois, o governo deveria ser assumido pelo presidente da Assembleia Legislativa, deputado Gerson Claro. No entanto, o parlamentar informou a Riedel que também estará ausente no período.

Com isso, Dorival Renato Pavan, terceiro na linha sucessória, assume o governo de Mato Grosso do Sul.

A assessoria de Gerson Claro informou que o deputado estará ausente por "compromissos de agenda".

A substituição está prevista no artigo 87 da Constituição Estadual. Segundo a regra, quando o governador e o vice-governador não podem exercer suas funções, o comando do estado passa para o presidente da Assembleia Legislativa e, depois, para o presidente do Tribunal de Justiça.

articles.title: Garupa morre e motociclista fica ferido após acidente em Itu | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a concessionária que administra a SP-280, o condutor do automóvel não visualizou a distância de segurança e colidiu contra a traseira da motocicleta, que tombou na pista.
articles.summary: Uma mulher morreu, neste domingo (1º), na rodovia Presidente Castello Branco, em Itu. Ela estava na garupa de uma moto atingida por um carro. O condutor teve ferimentos leves.
articles.body:
Colisão entre carro e moto na SP-280, em Itu (SP), provocou o tombamento do motociclista e da garupa, que foi socorrida, mas não resistiu aos ferimentos — Foto: Portal CCM – ARTESP (ccm.artesp.sp.gov.br)/Divulgação

Uma mulher morreu, neste domingo (1º), no quilômetro 66 da rodovia Presidente Castello Branco (SP-280), em Itu (SP). Ela estava na garupa de uma moto atingida por um carro. O condutor da motocicleta teve ferimentos leves.

De acordo com a concessionária que administra a rodovia, os veículos trafegavam no sentido oeste quando o condutor do automóvel bateu na traseira da moto.

Ainda segundo a concessionária, a colisão provocou o tombamento da motocicleta e dos ocupantes do veículo. A garupa chegou a ser socorrida, mas não resistiu. O motociclista assinou um termo de recusa de remoção médica.

O acostamento e duas faixas foram interditados e o tráfego ficou lento por cerca de dois quilômetros na região. Os veículos foram removidos do local.

articles.title: ‘He’s a force’: Obama answers call to boost Democrats – and rattle Trump
articles.summary: Former president has given series of blistering speeches to help candidates in key races – and deployment has proved a hit with party’s progressive wing
articles.body:
That could have been awkward. Barack Obama , campaigning for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, acknowledged that his fellow Democrat has criticised some aspects of the Obama presidency.

"Yeah, Abdul didn't agree with some things we wanted to do – that our administration was doing – when I was president," he told a rally in Detroit . "You know who else doesn't agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama." The crowd erupted in laughter. "I'd say about five times a day, she says, 'You knucklehead. Why you do that?'"

It was an elegant attempt to bridge the gap between the old Democratic party and the new. The US midterm elections have brought anti-incumbent sentiment to the fore. Some candidates have actively shrugged off their party labels , eager to cast themselves as outsiders running against the Washington establishment.

Against that backdrop, who wants a 65-year-old former president who left office nearly a decade ago with his promise of hope and change still only partly realised? It seems that Democrats do.

"Yes, we can!" chanted the crowd this week inside an arena in suburban Atlanta, Georgia, reviving the cadence of an Obama 2008 campaign that now feels like an artefact from a vanished age.

With days to go before midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump's second term, Democrats have turned to their most formidable orator for a series of blistering speeches in the campaign's closing days.

America's first Black president has mercilessly mocked Trump's autocratic pretensions and derided his foreign policy misadventures in the Middle East.

"This election is our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration," he said in Georgia. "It's the circuit-breaker in the system, and we need to flip it."

For party strategists, the decision to deploy Obama in the campaign's closing stretch was a calculated gamble. Unlike Trump, who has spent weeks staging grievance-filled rallies in traditional Republican strongholds, Obama maintained a selective public profile until the final weeks, allowing a new generation of Democratic candidates to establish their own identities before delivering a late burst of star power.

David Litt, a former Obama White House speechwriter, said: "What you're seeing is him coming in to support a new generation of Democratic leaders who have emerged organically, rather than trying to be involved from day one. He still has both a credibility and an ability to drive turnout that, if you're a candidate in a close race, you can absolutely benefit from – especially among young voters and Black voters."

The former president possesses a rare currency in modern US politics, according to Litt: the ability to command attention, and unnerve his successor.

"Obama is good at getting attention, and attention is hard to get these days," he continued. "The other thing is he continues to live in Trump's head rent-free. Donald Trump is out there on the stump, and in theory, he should be talking about his accomplishments. Instead he's relitigating his decisions involving ballroom renovations, because he can't help but get triggered by a single sentence from a former president."

That sentence came at a rally in Cleveland, Ohio, when Obama observed that Trump's gold-encrusted renovations have left the White House looking as if "Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory".

The comment triggered a mini-culture war in rightwing media – not because Obama had invoked a murderous Iraqi dictator, but because he had dared to suggest that a popular restaurant chain was a symbol of vulgar excess.

Trump waved his arms to mimic a lettuce leaf, accused Obama of snobbery and said : "Every piece of lettuce he eats has to be perfect, and I'm not that choosy." He defended his gilded White House decor and claimed Obama had left the executive mansion "deteriorated".

Trump's treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, a wealthy former hedge fund manager, even staged a photo-op outside a Cheesecake Factory in Washington, ordering a french-dip cheeseburger in an apparent attempt to rebut accusations of elitism and urging "the Martha's Vineyard set" to sample the chain's multi-page menu.

To Obama, the outcry merely proved his case. In Atlanta, he said: "They mobilised a whole-of-government response to a joke, not to inflation, but to a joke. They don't have solutions to actual problems, so they'd rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory."

For Litt, the Republican outrage betrayed a glaring double standard. "This is a party that spent years complaining, 'Oh, you're not allowed to say anything offensive any more,'" he said. "It turns out all these people who would die on the hill of allowing someone to use offensive language suddenly think [the] Cheesecake Factory is a line you just can't cross."

In rural east Tennessee, Corbin Trent, a media strategist and former communications director for Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, scoffed at Republican attempts to portray Obama's remarks as elite condescension toward working people.

He said: "They thought they were going to do this liberal elite stuff. I live in rural America. You've got this guy, Donald Trump, who presents himself like a mafioso, running our country like a mob – how can he enrich himself? There's no accountability. You're reminded of it every time you go to the grocery store, fill up your gas tank, turn on the TV and see that we're bombing more places."

Democrats have also mobilised former vice-president Kamala Harris for their midterm effort, while ex-president Bill Clinton campaigned with David Jolly , who is running for governor of Florida. But Obama has been unusually active in presidential, congressional and gubernatorial elections since he left the White House.

In 2024 he backed Harris in the final stretch of the presidential race, which Trump ultimately won. When Obama opened his presidential centre in Chicago in June, all living former presidents were in attendance – but Trump was not.

Yet within the broader Democratic coalition, Obama's legacy remains complicated. For a younger generation of activists who came of age during Bernie Sanders' presidential campaigns and the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the former president is remembered as much for his institutional constraints and moderate compromises as for his inspirational rhetoric.

Norman Solomon , a co-founder of the progressive group RootsAction, said: "It's like a great oil painting. If you walk up to it and look real close, it's not going to look so great. If you look too close at Obama's record – the collapse on peacemaking in Palestine, tripling troops in Afghanistan, presiding over the greatest upward transfer of wealth in anybody's lifetime – it does not look so great.

"Then he leaves the White House and jets off to an island owned by a billionaire [the Obamas spent a post-presidency vacation on private islands owned by the British billionaire Sir Richard Branson in 2017]. That is not solidarity."

Solomon acknowledged, however, that in the immediate crisis of 2026, Obama's tactical value is undeniable. "Almost anybody is going to look great compared to Trump. In Michigan, where there's been resentment between African American and Arab American communities, it's helpful for Obama to present a wiser outlook on what's at stake."

Other progressives welcome Obama back on the campaign trail, seeing his involvement not as a concession to the old order, but as evidence that the former president recognises how far the party has moved to the left.

Joseph Geevarghese , executive director of Our Revolution, a group that grew out of Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign, said: "Obama hitting the campaign trail is a net positive because it's strategic. He helps pull in key demographics including African American voters.

"But more broadly, I interpret Obama being on the campaign trail as a validation of the progressive movement's momentum. He is the epitome of the establishment, and he is out there pounding the pavement for progressives, saying our agenda isn't radical – it's mainstream. It's an affirmation of how powerful our movement has become."

Geevarghese also highlighted Obama's ability to shield minority candidates from xenophobic attacks. "Obama represents a candidate who overcame the opposition's 'othering' – when they called him un-American and used his middle name, Hussein. In the case of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who is weathering some of those same attacks, having Obama on the trail validates his candidacy and bolsters him within the American mainstream."

Since 2016, the DSA has grown from 6,000 members to over 130,000 nationwide, scoring high-profile mayoral victories with Zohran Mamdani in New York while looking to expand its congressional caucus.

Ashik Siddique , co-chair of the DSA, said: "Today, Obama appearing alongside progressive candidates shows where the decisive shift is happening. Voters want real results toward an alternative to the factors that produced Donald Trump. Barack Obama coming out and campaigning with candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan shows a recognition of where voters are."

Yet Obama, like Trump, remains a political unicorn: a figure who defies easy categorisation. That remains a strength. Nina Turner , a former Ohio state senator and prominent progressive voice, said: "President Obama, because of his uniqueness, transcends the anti-establishment movement."

"He is still an extraordinarily positive figure among the Democratic base," she added. "Even on the progressive side, for those of us who were disappointed with the ultimate analysis of his presidency – the drone wars, running on hope and change but not making a whole lot of change – he still has 'that thing.' He's a force."

"The critique of President Obama is he was very much establishment: he ran on hope and change, but didn't make a whole lot of change," said Turner. "People were hopeful, though, and it's the hopeful portion of his candidacy that still looms large – even as people critique his presidency, particularly on the progressive side of the ledger. Overall him being out there will be good for Democrats of all generations."

articles.title: Hegseth digs in as confident Democrats plan to go on offense after midterms
articles.summary: Earlier this year, Senate Republicans decided to tighten the screws on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The Pentagon had, for months, stonewalled lawmakers' r...
articles.body:
Earlier this year, Senate Republicans decided to tighten the screws on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The Pentagon had, for months, stonewalled lawmakers' request for materials related to the military's deadly targeting of alleged drug traffickers in Latin America. So this spring, the GOP-led Senate Armed Services Committee made a threat: grant access to the documents or it would block one of the Trump administration's political nominees.

Hegseth relented, said two people familiar with the exchange, speaking like some others on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations and the secretary's standing with Congress.

Spokespeople for the committee and the Pentagon declined to address questions about the episode.

The standoff, which has not been previously reported, illustrates Hegseth's increasing susceptibility to congressional oversight and how he might attempt to navigate a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill should Democrats prevail in this week's midterm elections.

With limited exception, Republican lawmakers have declined to stand in Hegseth's way while he has purged dozens of senior military leaders he's deemed disloyal, waged an eight-month war in Iran without the consent of Congress and pursued an unprecedented campaign against the illicit drug trade.

Democrats would give Hegseth far less room for maneuver once the next Congress convenes in January. Already, some are threatening to investigate and try to remove him from office if they reclaim a majority.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement that, "despite threats of sham witch hunts," Hegseth is "100% committed" to leading the Defense Department "until the end" of President Donald Trump's term and to advancing the president's agenda for the military.

The secretary "will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists," Parnell said, adding that the department under Hegseth "has followed the law."

Rep. Adam Smith (Washington), the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said in an interview that, as chairman, he would probe three areas: military operations, politicization of the armed forces and potential corruption in the Pentagon's awarding of defense contracts.

The Defense Department is readying for such inquires. Those preparations include accounting for the likelihood that if Democrats take charge they will summon military officers to testify on Capitol Hill, people familiar with the matter said.

Hegseth faces a more imminent challenge, though. When lawmakers return to Washington later this month, the House will probably vote on an effort to impeach him over the Iran war. That effort is being led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie (Kentucky), a frequent critic of the administration.

"There's a decent chance that it could pass the House, and I think that would be a stain on his record," Massie said in an interview. "If he's contemplating leaving, this would be a good time to do it."

The House vote is expected to be close, but the effort is highly unlikely to result in a conviction if it advances to the Senate for a trial.

Some officials in the administration and in Congress have mused recently that Hegseth may leave the Pentagon if Republicans lose heavily in the midterms - either to avoid congressional scrutiny or to pursue potential political ambitions. It's possible, too, that the president could remove Hegseth if voters punish the GOP over the Iran war, though Trump has said he stands by him.

Two people familiar with Hegseth's thinking said the secretary wants to stay in office for four years. One said it's "silly" to think Democrats having greater control on Capitol Hill will change that.

The other person said that Hegseth's September address to hundreds of service members in Quantico, Virginia, was meant to be a road map for his next two years in office, including priorities such as building a new U.S. military base and adopting advanced weaponry.

An impeachment would be difficult for Hegseth if he does not stay in office, with significant legal costs and less control over what the Defense Department provides to congressional investigators, another person said.

Asked by a reporter Thursday about the prospect of an impeachment, Trump - twice impeached himself - called the threat against Hegseth "terrible" and repeated his confidence in the secretary.

"He's a great warrior," the president said.

Some Democrats acknowledged being concerned that, should they regain a majority in Congress, repeatedly targeting Hegseth could imperil their ability to compromise with Republicans on critical defense legislation. Still, many of those who sit on the committees that oversee the Pentagon say that Hegseth hasn't worked with them for his two years in office.

"Since I became ranking member, I have had the cellphone number of every single secretary of defense," said Smith, who has held the prominent House role for nearly 16 years. "Hegseth does not speak to me."

Others in the party have vowed to oust Hegseth.

Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colorado), told reporters in October that he would do "everything possible" to remove Hegseth if Democrats retake the House.

Hegseth's defenders say they loathe the thought of Trump giving the Democrats "a scalp" by forcing him out, one administration official said.

With the president's support, Hegseth has survived multiple controversies, including his use of the commercial messaging app Signal to share highly sensitive details on an imminent military strike and the military's decision to kill two people who survived a strike on an alleged drug boat.

But in recent weeks, members of both parties have grown more willing to confront Hegseth, signaling they will block his preferred choices to lead the Army and denouncing his call to live-stream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who committed a mass killing at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

Current and former officials familiar with the Pentagon's standing on Capitol Hill said that Hegseth's challenge after the midterms will be to shore up bipartisan support for the military and defend his record as lawmakers from both parties have grown more critical of him.

Two of the officials asserted that Hegseth could work across party lines, depending on how aggressive Democrats were in their investigations. Still, several others predicted that his critics, both in Congress and in the Pentagon, could feel more emboldened to oppose him if Democrats take power.

"Pete has made so many enemies - and uncontrollable enemies," one person familiar said.

articles.title: Fox News Power Rankings: Kansas moves to Toss-up, Nebraska moves to Lean R
articles.summary: The Ohio Senate race shifts to Lean D as Sherrod Brown leads Jon Husted, while Kansas and South Carolina move to toss-up in the final rankings.
articles.body: Updated Nov. 1: We’re updating this forecast to move Kansas from Lean R to Toss-up, and Nebraska from Likely R to Lean R. Kansas is a conservative stronghold, but Republicans are spending too much time and money relative to other states to conclude that Sen. Roger Marshall has an edge over Democrat Adam Hamilton. The odds remain in Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts' favor in Nebraska. A larger-than-expected swing against the GOP could open the door for independent Dan Osborn to pull off an upset. We still consider Senate control a toss-up. Seven states are most likely to decide the majority. On a good night for the Democrats, their ceiling rises to 55 seats. A good night for the Republicans could see them retain control with up to 52 seats. TRUMP-BACKED SENATOR ADMITS GOP FACES NIGHTMARE SCENARIO IN STATE REPUBLICANS HAVEN'T LOST IN 90 YEARS — As Iran looms large, can the GOP keep the faithful? It seems like there are two electorates in these midterms. SCHOEN, COOPERMAN: DEMOCRATS COULD BE RIDING A MIDTERM WAVE. THESE NUMBERS SHOULD TERRIFY THE GOP The first is frustrated with President Donald Trump and ready to reject Republicans. It includes growing numbers of independent, rural and Hispanic voters who say they’ll vote for a Democrat. That’s what the latest round of House polling shows, including a survey last week that had Democrats up 11 points on the generic ballot, and Fox’s most recent national poll. The second electorate is wavering on Republicans but won’t necessarily hand Democrats the Senate. These are the voters in the Midwest and a few other places. They say they prefer the Democrat or Republican in their states by a point or two at most. That’s the right conclusion from most of the battleground Senate polling. How could both things be true? In other words, if Democrats have such a wide lead in the House, won’t the Senate fall too? Both are true, and a big lead in the House doesn’t necessarily translate to the Senate. These voters are all in the same electorate, and they only seem divorced from each other because the House and Senate maps are so far apart this year. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG? The president’s declining approval rating and Democratic advantages on the issues will likely deliver them the House, and possibly by many seats. Those advantages have also allowed the blue team to play in a lot of Senate races that Republicans thought were unreachable, but only to the point of making them battlegrounds. GOP SENATE MAJORITY FACES FRESH UNCERTAINTY AS 2 KEY RACES TIGHTEN DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS The road to a Senate majority goes through several states that Trump won by 11 points or more. Democrats can win any of these races. If Republicans turn out and stay loyal to their party, the climb for the left will be steep. That’s why the Senate is a toss-up. Voters could give Democrats a majority, and maybe with several seats to spare. They could also let the Republicans keep control. We’ll find out next week. Democrats have strong advantages on most key issues In his 11-year political career, Trump has triumphed over almost all the threats to his power. The exception was the coronavirus pandemic, which was the top issue for voters in the 2020 election and ushered in the Biden presidency. It was also one of the few threats that Trump has faced from abroad. This time, Trump and the Republicans face a new foreign opponent: Iran. The administration’s decision to start joint U.S.-Israeli military strikes against the nation in February has cast a shadow over the GOP. First, it has impacted Trump’s approval rating, which will decide the fate of many congressional Republicans and has fallen since the war began. It was 44% in the last pre-war survey and sits at 36% now. The war has also given Democrats advantages on the top issues. In Fox’s October survey, Iran played a role in four issues that more than two-thirds of voters said they were concerned about: inflation (85%), gas prices (83%), government leadership (79%), and the war in Iran itself (75%). Most voters said they preferred the Democrats to handle those issues: 16 points on inflation, 12 points on gas prices, 11 points on leadership, and 9 points on foreign policy. Republicans are competitive on home turf Still, voters are not convinced that the Senate should change hands. That comes down to the territory. Trump won seven of the 11 battleground states in 2024, and seven of them by double digits. That includes Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Democrats don’t need to win all of those states to take the Senate, but it’s hard to see how they get to 51 seats without at least two of them. While former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown leads in Ohio, the other states are close. Turnout, a polling error in either direction or both could decide them. There are also a lot of undecided voters. In Alaska, Iowa and Kansas, three states with recent high-quality polling, an average of 10% of voters say they haven’t decided who they will support or won’t support the major candidates. Any guess on how those voters will break at the ballot box is only a guess. All we know from prior results is that the overall electorate leans conservative, so the Democrats have the tougher assignment to bring them over to their side (or keep them at home). There are far fewer undecided voters in Texas, where last week’s Fox News Poll showed a tied race at 49%-49%. If Democrats only win two Trump-won battlegrounds, they’ll need to win three other races where former Vice President Kamala Harris delivered single-digit victories in 2024: Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire. Democrats are ahead in the latter two. Maine could go either way. While Democrats win its presidential races, it could just as easily be considered a Republican state when Susan Collins is on the ballot. Senate: Democrats are favored in 48 seats; Kansas moves to Toss-up and Nebraska moves to Lean R Both parties are short of a majority in this forecast. Democrats are favored in 48 seats and Republicans are ahead in 45. On a good night for Democrats, the party would win most or all the toss-ups, taking the majority with up to 55 seats. In that scenario, other competitive states would also come into focus, including Nebraska, and possibly Mississippi. A good night for the Republicans would see them simply hold on to most of the states they already have, up to a ceiling of 52 seats. The party also has opportunities to flip a couple of states, including Minnesota and New Hampshire. Five states have moved in Power Rankings forecasts this week. Ohio In Ohio, Brown has enjoyed a lead in three Fox News polls this year, including last week’s survey, which had him five points ahead of Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted at 52%-47%. Ohio voters are very familiar with Brown, having sent him to the Senate three times. That has made it hard for Husted to campaign on socialism and woke politics, themes that Republicans elsewhere see as their strongest cards to play. Ohio moves from Toss-up to Lean D. ("Lean D" means the Democrat has an edge, but it’s still a highly competitive race. We define every ranking and the process for setting them on FoxNews.com.) South Carolina As this week’s Power Rankings previously reported, Republicans already viewed this as an uncomfortably close race. That belief is now widely shared. The president headed back there to help Sen. Darline Graham in the Upstate, where she underperformed in her primary runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman. South Carolina moves from Lean R to Toss-up. Kansas Kansas is a conservative stronghold, but Republicans are spending too much time and money relative to other states to conclude that Sen. Roger Marshall has an edge over Democrat Adam Hamilton. Kansas moves from Lean R to Toss-up. Nebraska The odds remain in Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts' favor in Nebraska. A larger-than-expected swing against the GOP could open the door for independent Dan Osborn to pull off an upset. Nebraska moves from Likely R to Lean R. Mississippi Mississippi is a Republican stronghold, but Trump’s decision to rally there over other deep red states is a sign that the party thinks it’s competitive. GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith faces Democratic District Attorney Scott Colom in a race where protein choice has become a breakout issue. Mississippi moves from Solid R to Likely R. House: The floor for Democrats ticks up four seats to 223 Democrats are still likely to flip the House this November, and in this forecast, they’re predicted to take at least 223 seats. Since a good night for the Democrats would see them take most of the toss-up races, they could end up with as many as 240 seats. (On a great Democratic night, the party would pick up most of the Lean R districts as well, taking them as high as 252 seats.) Republicans have 195 seats in their columns. A good night for them would take that total up to around 212. That’s six short of a majority, but enough to make life difficult for the next Democratic House speaker, who would have to balance the demands of the moderate and far-left wings of the party. Nineteen more races have shifted in the Democrats’ direction this week, all on the same themes outlined in the last House update: national and district polling, top-of-the-ticket strength, and rural voter erosion. The earliest-closing districts on election night will give some sense of the House’s future. Keep an eye on Kentucky’s 6th District, which covers Lexington and a large central area of the state. Trump won here by 15 points in the last presidential election. Thanks to a combination of left-leaning college voters and farmers grappling with higher costs, it looks close this cycle. The district moves from Lean R to Toss-up. Governor: Ad or no ad, the Ohio governor’s race moves to Lean D Finally, Ohio’s gubernatorial race is also on the move. The campaign between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy was the top story in politics last week after Ramaswamy ran an ad featuring Acton’s mother, who called her daughter a liar. Acton has been estranged from her mother since age 12, when she says she and her brother left her family home because her mother’s husband was sexually abusing her. Acton’s brother now appears in a response ad discussing their family history. This ratings change is less about the response to the ad (Ramaswamy and President Trump are supportive of the commercial; most others, including Husted and Gov. Mike DeWine are against it) than it is about the fact that the Ramaswamy campaign felt the need to run it. While Ramaswamy sat only two points behind Acton in last week’s Fox poll, he’s an average of seven points behind in other high-quality polls since September. The businessman and onetime presidential hopeful has struggled in favorability ratings throughout his political career. This ad is unlikely to help. The Ohio governor’s race moves from Toss-up to Lean D. articles.title: Tim Scott declares alleged 'Decoy Dan' plot a 'criminal offense' as DOJ investigation rocks Alaska
articles.summary: NRSC chair Sen. Tim Scott says he feels "vindicated" after the Department of Justice reportedly issued dozens of subpoenas in Alaska's U.S. Senate race.
articles.body: National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) Chair Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., told Fox News he felt vindicated after the Department of Justice reportedly issued dozens of subpoenas in Alaska, arguing that Republicans had warned for months about an alleged Democratic effort to recruit a "decoy" U.S. Senate candidate. Speaking on "Saturday in America," Scott said the NRSC identified the alleged scheme early, accusing U.S. Senate candidate Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. of copying the campaign logos, colors and materials of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. "Absolutely vindicated. We've been saying this for months," Scott said Saturday. SCHUMER ACCUSED OF YEARLONG PLOT TO PLANT 'DECOY' CANDIDATE IN CRITICAL SENATE RACE "The truth is that the fake Dan, the 'Decoy Dan,' his one objective is to confuse voters. Number two, if there's a second point, it's the collusion that occurred to recruit this candidate. That is a criminal offense. It is immoral, frankly, to lie to the public about who you are, but it is actually illegal to collude with others in order to confuse the voters," he added. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign, along with senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, were involved in an alleged effort to recruit a candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent. The alleged effort was intended to confuse voters and draw support away from Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to the report. MARY PELTOLA TRASHES NEW YORK TIMES REPORT ON DAN SULLIVAN PLOT, CALLING IT A 'DISTRACTION' Peltola said she "knew nothing" about an alleged scheme to recruit a candidate with the same name as her opponent to run in the election. Sen. Dan Sullivan, however, told Fox News she is "still lying." In a statement to Fox News Digital, Peltola's campaign denied any involvement in the alleged scheme. "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign," the campaign said. "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first — and no threats from DC politicians or baseless investigations from a weaponized Department of Justice will keep her away from that fight." The two candidates appear on the ballot under similar names. The incumbent Republican senator is listed as "Sullivan, Dan S.," while Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher running without party affiliation, is listed as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." In an interview with The Associated Press published in June, Sullivan Jr. denied being a spoiler candidate and said he entered the race independently. PELTOLA CAMPAIGN'S ALLEGED DAN SULLIVAN SPOILER PLOT TAKES NEW TURN AS DOJ FACES MAJOR LEGAL HURDLE "Every single piece of his campaign information copied the real Dan Sullivan's logo, the colors and even the font. He tried to change his middle initial so that he could confuse more voters as if he was the real Dan Sullivan — all that with 30 subpoenas means he could be in serious federal trouble," Scott said. Scott also pointed to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings as evidence of what he described as a sham candidacy, arguing that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had made little effort to mount a serious campaign for the U.S. Senate seat. TRUMP PROSECUTIONS UNDER BIDEN SET PRECEDENT FOR DOJ’S ALASKA ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE, EX-FEC CHAIR SAYS "On his FEC forms, federal election forms, what does he show? Nothing," Scott said. "He's actually done nothing trying to achieve the goal of being the senator. He's done one thing, which is to put his name on the ballot to confuse the voters." Scott also warned that the alleged decoy candidate could face legal consequences if he lies to federal investigators. SCHIFF ACCUSES DOJ OF TRYING TO 'SUBVERT' ELECTIONS AS GOP ALLEGES SAME-NAME CANDIDATE MEANT TO CONFUSE VOTERS "I would be shaking in my boots if I was 'Decoy Dan,' and frankly, no one wants to go to jail for something they didn't do," Scott said. "So he'd be very careful as he talks to the federal Department of Justice about what happened and what didn't happen. Lying to the prosecutors — that's a felony." Fox News Digital reached out to Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for comment. articles.title: The DSA welcomes you to the $47 trillion waiting room
articles.summary: Rep. Harriet Hageman warned that the Democratic Socialists of America’s proposed nationalized healthcare plan would significantly increase taxes, lengthen wait times, and threaten the stability of rural hospitals.
articles.body:
The Democratic Socialists of America organization’s policies will close rural hospitals and force Americans to bankroll gender experimentation surgeries on children. Their proposal to nationalize healthcare under the so-called “Medicare for All” proposal is just the beginning of a dangerous path down a dystopian future under their socialist agenda.

Seeing a specialist in Wyoming typically involves a two-hour drive. Socialist single-payer healthcare promises to add a lengthy waiting list on top of excessive travel time, while sending the bill to every taxpayer.

That is not hyperbole. The White House Council of Economic Advisers recently released a report, “ The Real Cost of Socialism in America ,” outlining the consequences of the Democratic Socialists of America agenda. Single-payer healthcare accounts for $47.4 trillion of the roughly $49 trillion their plan would add to the deficit over the next decade. Of the eight socialist policies examined, the net fiscal burden would cost $355,000 per American household. The largest comes from the Medicare for All proposal.

Republicans in Washington have already demonstrated a better way. Last year, Congress delivered a historic $50 billion investment in rural healthcare through the One Big Beautiful Bill for Wyoming, that means a $205 million investment through the Rural Health Transformation Program to help address long-standing challenges specific to rural residents.

The Rural Health Transformation Program represents the largest targeted federal investment in rural healthcare in American history, supporting expanded primary, preventive, maternal, emergency, and behavioral health services, recruitment and retention of a strong rural health workforce, and modernized facilities and technology.

Rather than imposing a one-size-fits all solution crafted by Washington bureaucrats, Republicans recognize that rural communities face unique challenges that require locally led solutions. We stand to lose this progress if the radical left gains power.

The socialists’ Medicare for All agenda would fundamentally transform how Americans receive and pay for healthcare. In order to achieve zero-dollar premiums and cost sharing, this plan increases taxes on the middle class and forces every American to enroll in a government-run healthcare system, taking away people’s healthcare choices. This is the same bait and switch Democrats used to enact ObamaCare: promise affordable healthcare services and access, but then deliver higher taxes, individual mandates and limited access.

That means tens of thousands of Wyoming workers who rely on carefully negotiated benefits through major local industries, such as energy and mining, would see their preferred private plans abolished in favor of a federal one-size-fits-all program.

Part of Medicare for All’s coverage would also force Americans to bankroll gender experimentation surgeries, even if they have conscientious objections. The Council of Economic Advisers estimates these surgeries could cost taxpayers $68 billion over the ten-year period. The proposal would also extend government-funded healthcare eligibility to illegal immigrants, further increasing costs for law-abiding Americans.

The greatest concern is what Medicare for All means for our rural hospitals. Private commercial insurance helps cross-subsidize the losses our rural hospitals incur from government programs. Under the Medicare for All proposal, the private insurance buffer would disappear as reimbursements shift towards government-set rates. Wyoming’s Critical Access Hospitals, which serve communities separated by vast distances, already operate on thin margins. A sharp reduction in reimbursement would force these facilities to eliminate specialized services, downsize emergency departments, reduce staff, and in the worst cases, close their doors.

Even for hospitals that do remain open, many patients could face longer wait times if Medicare for All becomes our reality. Wyoming already faces a shortage of primary care doctors and medical specialists. The supply of doctors, specialists, diagnostic equipment, and hospital capacity does not suddenly increase to meet higher demand for care. Something has to give, which is usually the amount of time patients have to wait for services. Single-payer systems around the world feature wait times weeks and even years longer than the U.S. for routine medical services.

As we know, when socialists say something is “free,” they usually mean for illegal aliens, not American taxpayers who would ultimately bear the burden of implementing their costly agenda. For Wyoming taxpayers, the required federal tax spike would hit local working families uniquely hard. Analyses from non-partisan organizations, like the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget , have noted that many middle-class workers could end up paying more in newly added taxes than they previously saved on healthcare premiums.

Instead of dismantling private coverage and putting every American into a government-run system, we should continue investing in rural hospitals, strengthening the healthcare workforce, expanding access to innovative technologies, and giving states the flexibility to develop solutions that meet the needs of their communities, which is exactly what the Rural Health Transformation Program does.

Socialists promise free healthcare, but Wyoming would pay for it twice, first in taxes and then in time spent waiting. The choice for Wyoming families should be clear: protect healthcare freedom rather than surrender control of your healthcare decisions to the Democratic Socialists of America.

Harriet Hageman represents Wyoming at large in Congress and is the Article One Task Force Chair for the Republican Study Committee.

articles.title: Everything to know about House and Senate control, ballot measures and 2026 Election Day poll closing
articles.summary: Republicans defend slim congressional majorities as toss-up Senate races in Alaska, Texas and Iowa could decide control of the chamber in 2026.
articles.body: In two days, Americans voting in the midterm elections will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate for the next two years. Republicans are defending their slim congressional majorities, but President Donald Trump predicts the GOP will hold the House and Senate. "If you elect a Republican House and a Republican Senate on Nov. 3, we will continue to put America first every single day," the president pledged on the campaign trail last week. And he claimed if the Democrats take control, "this country will go to hell." CHECK OUT THE FINAL FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Republicans are fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. The GOP also faces a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation tied in part to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings. Also up for grabs in this year's midterm elections — governorships in 36 of the 50 states (as well as the territories of Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands). Plus, all but four states are holding legislative elections. And voters will also weigh in on 145 statewide ballot measures in states from coast to coast. Here's a closer look at what's up for grabs on Election Day 2026. SENATE Republicans currently control the chamber 53-47, with the final Fox News Power Rankings ahead of Election Day rating the race for Senate control a toss-up. Both parties are three seats short of a majority, according to the forecast. Democrats are favored in 48 seats and Republicans are ahead in 47. The GOP needs to hold 50 seats to retain control of the chamber, since Republican Vice President JD Vance is the tie-breaking vote in the Senate. WHO'S UP AND DOWN IN THE FINAL FOX NEWS MIDTERM ELECTION POLLS If Democrats ride a blue wave to victory by winning most or all of the competitive races, they could potentially come away from the midterms with up to 54 seats. But if Republicans have a good night and defy expectations, the GOP could hold the majority with up to 52 seats, according to the forecast. Republicans are playing defense in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, South Carolina and Texas, which are all rated toss-ups in the Power Rankings. They're also defending seats in competitive races in Kansas, which is rated Lean Republican, and Ohio, which is rated Lean Democrat. Democrats are on defense in Michigan, which is rated a toss-up, and in Minnesota and New Hampshire, which are listed as Lean Democrat. HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES The GOP is hanging on to a razor-thin majority in the House, and the Power Rankings point to the Democrats retaking control of the chamber. A good night for the Democrats could see them ending up with as many as 240 seats in the 435-seat chamber. But if Republicans have a good night, they could end up with 212 seats. That’s six short of a majority, but enough to make life difficult for the next Democratic House speaker, who would have to balance the demands of the moderate and far-left wings of the party. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The earliest-closing districts on election night will give some sense of the House’s future. "Keep an eye on Kentucky’s 6th District, which covers Lexington and a large central area of the state. Trump won here by 15 points in the last presidential election. Thanks to a combination of left-leaning college voters and farmers grappling with higher costs, it looks close this cycle," Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings, said. GOVERNORS There are currently 26 Republican and 24 Democratic governors. The Power Rankings list three states where the GOP controls the governor's office – Alaska, Nevada and Georgia – as toss-ups. Wisconsin, which has an open Democratic-controlled governor's office, is also rated a toss-up. The gubernatorial races in red states Florida, Kansas and Texas are rated Lean Republican, according to the Power Rankings. DEMOCRACY 2026: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Five other races are also seen as competitive and rated Lean Democrat. They are Arizona, Michigan and Oregon, where Democrats are playing defense, and Iowa and Ohio, where the GOP is defending open governor's offices. BALLOT MEASURES Referendums requiring voters to present identification when they show up at the polls, or bans on noncitizen voting, are on the ballot in 11 states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Kansas, Nevada, North Carolina, Ohio, South Dakota and West Virginia. Voters in Alaska will also decide if they want to repeal the state’s ranked choice voting system, open primaries and a campaign finance disclosure rule. Voters approved the current system in 2020 and narrowly kept it in 2024. But the voting system has come under fresh scrutiny amid the controversy over a potential spoiler candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race. Voters in Virginia will decide whether the right to vote should be restored to convicted felons upon their release. California's Proposition 40 is making national headlines. The measure, the first of its kind, would slap a one-time 5% tax on wealth for Californians worth over $1 billion, with the vast majority of the revenue generated going to pay for healthcare. Also in the spotlight is a millionaires' tax in Washington state. If passed, the referendum would repeal a 9.9% tax on income over $1 million a year, which state lawmakers recently approved. Washington state currently does not have a personal income tax. Voters in Maryland, Missouri and Colorado weigh in on ballot measures on congressional redistricting, as the mid-decade redistricting fight between Democrats and Republicans will be waged again in 2028. Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington state have referendums on transgender students’ participation in sports. Colorado also has a referendum on blocking gender transition surgeries for minors and preventing state or federal funding from being used for those operations. Voters in Missouri weigh in on repealing a right to abortion and banning gender transition medical care for children. Meanwhile, an Idaho initiative would overturn one of the nation's strictest abortion bans, while Virginia and Nevada voters decide on establishing a right to abortion in their state constitutions. California, Colorado and Arizona hold ballot measures on policy around energy, transportation and development. POLL CLOSINGS The first poll closings come at 6 p.m. ET on Election Day, with the final poll closings happening at 1 a.m. ET. 6 p.m. ET: Polls close in parts of Kentucky and Indiana. 7 p.m. ET: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia. The final polls in Kentucky and Indiana close. And most polls in Florida and New Hampshire close. 7:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia. 8 p.m. ET: Polls close in Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee and Washington, D.C. The remaining polls in Florida and New Hampshire close. Most polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota. 8:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arkansas. 9 p.m. PT: Polls close in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming. The final polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota. 10 p.m. ET: Polls close in Montana and Utah. Most polls also close in Idaho and Oregon.
