Midnight ET: Polls in all of Hawaii and most of Alaska close, with the remaining polls in Alaska closing at 1 a.m. ET.

articles.title: Americans forced to change clocks again as Senate stalls Trump-backed daylight saving time bill
articles.summary: Trump shared Sen. Tom Cotton's cellphone number to pressure him on the Daylight Saving Time bill, but the Senate still has no clear path forward.
articles.body: Daylight saving time has dodged the wrath of President Donald Trump — for now. As Americans again participate in the twice-yearly ritual of fiddling with their clocks — this time rolling back an hour on Sunday morning — Congress has fallen short of tackling the issue in time. Earlier this year, the House passed legislation that would allow states to voluntarily observe daylight saving time year-round. But progress on the legislation has ground to a halt in the Senate, even though it’s a popular issue with voters and Trump. BATTLE OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME ERUPTS AS PUSH TO STOP CHANGING CLOCKS HITS SENATE WALL But it’s not for lack of trying. Trump has routinely pressured the upper chamber to pass the bill and re-upped that call earlier this week in the midst of traveling across the country to rally in key states and safe red bastions to urge voters to keep Republicans in power. "The United States Senate is letting the daylight saving bill die when a vast Majority of the Country want it," Trump said on Truth Social. "Most people are demanding light in the evening, but ALL want not to change their clocks anymore. TAKE A VOTE!" Trump wants the Senate to pass, or at least take a vote on, the Sunshine Protection Act, but it’s facing heavy headwinds from a broad swathe of lawmakers in the upper chamber on both sides of the aisle. TRUMP FACES REPUBLICAN REBELLION OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME AS SENATE BILL NEARS DEAD END His pressure campaign got to the point that he shared the cellphone number of one of his top allies, Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., one of the more vocal opponents of the bill, urging supporters to call the lawmaker and demand he work on passing the bill. "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Saving Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton said in response. "Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first." The House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act along bipartisan lines in July. Majorities of Democrats and Republicans voted in favor of the bill, which passed 307 to 117. Just 22 Republicans and 95 Democrats opposed it. But it’s one of several pieces of legislation that House lawmakers complain has fallen by the wayside in the upper chamber. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., pressed the Senate to take up that bill in comments to Fox News Digital in early October. TIME ENOUGH AT LAST: WHAT'S NEXT AFTER THE HOUSE PASSES BILL TO DO AWAY WITH DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME? Scalise told Fox News Digital, "There's no reason Americans should lose an hour of sunlight at the end of the day when more daylight means more time with our families, more activity for our businesses and safer communities." "President Trump has been pushing to make daylight saving time permanent, and House Republicans delivered by overwhelmingly passing the Sunshine Protection Act. It's a commonsense change and the Senate should take it up," Scalise said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And when the Senate returns after the election, lawmakers will have a densely packed schedule crammed with leftover legislation. With floor time being the top commodity in the upper chamber, squeezing the Sunshine Protection Act onto the floor may be a challenge, even without the resistance it already faces. "The president feels strongly on it like he does a lot of issues," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters earlier this month. "It’s something we’re having conversations about, but there’s no clear path forward or consensus on it yet."

articles.title: Poll: Voters demand change and a check on Trump, fueling a steep Democratic midterm advantage
articles.summary: Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump.
articles.body: Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump. Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents. Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture. When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — which is notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain. But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark in the NBC News poll across his two terms, and his approval rating stands at 40%. After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data. And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%). “The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies. Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war. Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year. Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security. “Democrats are in total control of the 2026 issue agenda,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, noting that only voters who think immigration is a top issue are breaking for his party right now. Democrats have a 1-point advantage on which party would better control inflation, a slight decline from September but still a warning sign for the GOP, which led on the issue in 2024. Republicans have a 2-point advantage on the economy, a marked decline from the party’s double-digit advantage on the issue in recent years. Voters are also signaling that they are fired up about the midterms, with 70% ranking themselves as a “9” or “10” on a 10-point scale of interest in the election. Democrats have a 12-point advantage among those most-engaged voters, while Republicans have a 2-point edge among voters who are less interested in the election. Self-described MAGA Republicans also say they’re significantly more interested in the election than Republicans who don’t identify with the MAGA wing, as Trump and his party push to turn out voters who typically sit out midterm elections. That dynamic could be one reason why Republicans have leaned into culture war arguments in key races, attacking Democrats on transgender issues. The new poll shows a potential limitation of that strategy: Democrats have a 5-point advantage on the question of which party would better handle transgender issues, despite those Republican attacks. It’s not all good news for Democrats, and the poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party, which remains deeply unpopular. Just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively, while 38% have positive views of the Republican Party. Around half of voters have negative views of both parties. Still, some voters who are wary of Democrats are still planning to support them this year. “Republicans have proven that they are not to be trusted. So I would rather see the balance of power shift, than maintain one party’s control,” one poll respondent from Texas, who voted for Trump in 2024 and is supporting Democrats for Congress this year, said in an expanded response. “I don’t trust Republicans or Democrats, really,” the man added. Republican disappointment Frustrations among voters like that man from Texas, who backed Trump in 2024 and typically backs Republicans, are dragging down the president and GOP candidates this year. Republicans are torn on whether the country is moving in the right direction (48%), or the wrong direction (43%). One year ago, Republicans said the country was going in the right direction, 75%-24%. Now, a majority of Republicans (53%) are dissatisfied with the state of the economy. And 37% of Trump’s own party believe he’s fallen short of his promises. Trump still maintains an important hold on his base, with near-unanimous job approval (93%) among Republicans who say they support the MAGA movement. But he’s slipped significantly with Republicans who don’t consider themselves part of the MAGA movement: 54% of them approve and 46% disapprove of his performance. Meanwhile, 20% of those non-MAGA Republicans say they prefer to see Democrats control Congress after this election. The president has seen other important voting blocs drift away, too. His net approval rating has dropped 18 points among white voters without college degrees compared to the first NBC News poll of his second term, in 2025. He’s also seen significant declines among young voters and Latino voters, groups that he overperformed with on his way back to the White House in 2024. One of Republicans’ big advantages in 2026 is a favorable political map: Democrats have to win back districts and states Trump won in 2024 to take back Congress. In the Senate, they need to win at least two states Trump carried by double-digit margins. But the president’s approval rating is underwater in states he won in 2024: 53% of registered voters there disapprove of his job performance, while 47% approve. In March 2025, his approval rating in those states was 10 points higher. Democratic warning signs There are some warning signs for Democrats, on top of the fact that a lower share of voters have positive views of the Democratic Party compared to the Republican Party. The fight for control of the House and especially the Senate will take place in Trump-won areas, and Republicans are leading on the congressional ballot in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024. The big question is whether that’s enough to withstand shifts in some key places. Government corruption has been a central theme of Democrats’ message this year, but voters narrowly trust Republicans to better handle the issue by 5 points. Even so, Democrats are leading on the congressional ballot among the 28% of voters who do not trust either party on the issue. Republican leaders in Congress are also slightly better off than their Democratic counterparts, but that’s mostly because voters don’t know how to feel about them. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has the highest positive rating of congressional leaders: 24% have positive views of him and 34% have negative views. Just 10% of voters have positive views of Johnson’s counterpart across the Capitol, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, while 22% view him negatively. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is viewed positively by 18% of voters and negatively by 35%. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who’s led Democrats in the body for almost a decade, is far better defined — to his detriment. Just 13% of voters view him positively, and 53% view him negatively. “It’s not great for the Democrats … for 2028,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, when asked about the low marks for Democrats. “But I don’t see it as a barrier for how well they can do in 2026 when midterms are about Trump and these economic numbers.” Half of voters have negative views of tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has emerged as one of the most prolific Republican donors in the country over the last two years, while 34% view him positively. Voters are more split about a pair of prominent progressives, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Sanders is more popular: 41% view him positively and 42% view him negatively, while Ocasio-Cortez’s numbers stand at 31%-42%. Democrats hold a significant lead in the battle for Congress despite those factors. But there are indications throughout the poll that the party’s lead is propped up strongly by anti-Republican sentiment, not warm feelings for Democrats. Voters who want Democratic control of Congress are divided between whether their vote is more in favor of Democrats or driven more by opposition to Republicans. “Get your s--- together, Democrats,” an Ohio Democratic woman said when asked what message she wanted to send with her vote this year. “I’m voting for you, but work it out.” The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Oct. 28-30 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

articles.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Pope Leo XIV casts ballot in US election, raising questions about foreign leaders voting
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV mailed an absentee ballot to Will County, Illinois, raising novel legal questions about a foreign head of state voting in U.S. elections.
articles.body: "So, the pope doesn’t take sides. Prevost has another opinion, but we won’t do that now." That funny quip from Pope Leo XIV, born Robert Prevost, referred to the historic game in Rome when the Villanova and Notre Dame basketball teams played each other. However, a story this week raised a different question of when the pope, as opposed to Prevost, can "take sides." POPE LEO MEETS WITH CHICAGO'S FAR-LEFT MAYOR, GEORGE FLOYD'S FAMILY LAWYER AT THE VATICAN This month, American-born Leo XIV became the first pope ever to vote in a U.S. election. A longtime Chicago native, the pope mailed an absentee ballot to Will County, and the clerk’s office confirmed to Fox News Digital that "Robert Prevost is on the list of individuals who requested a Vote by Mail ballot." There is no question that the pope can vote in the Holy See. Indeed, he is the ultimate and final vote in the Vatican, but can he actually vote in Illinois races — including the governor’s race involving incumbent Democrat JB Pritzker? The answer appears to be yes, but it raises some novel questions. Now, as a threshold matter, I want to shed some bias. I was raised Catholic in Chicago. No, that is not the bias. There is that lingering conflict with the pope coming out as a White Sox fan. Many of us on the North Side hoped for a conversion to restore our faith in papal infallibility. However, he has remained entrenched in his South Side allegiance. This column rises above that historic rivalry and does not suggest that White Sox fans can be challenged at the polls. Besides, I previously explained that the pope is a Cubs fan without knowing it. CHICAGO MAYOR JOHNSON HOPES TO ENLIST POPE IN REPARATIONS FIGHT AFTER HE APOLOGIZED FOR 'SCOURGE OF SLAVERY' Rather, what surprised me was that the head of a foreign state could vote in U.S. elections. The Vatican is a distinct nation with a diplomatic corps, a court system, a local government, and even a military in the form of the legendary Swiss Guards. The Holy See Press Office declared, "Pope Leo XIV has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen whenever he was eligible to do so. The Holy See Press Office confirms that, in keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago." The Holy See maintains that Pope Leo retains his status as a U.S. citizen while serving as the head of a foreign nation. There is support for this position. The State Department has maintained that dual citizens do not have to choose between their countries, though it does not expect them to serve as the head of another country. "U.S. dual nationals owe allegiance to both the United States and the foreign country (or countries, if they are nationals of more than one). They are required to obey the laws of both countries, and either country has the right to enforce its laws. Claims of other countries upon U.S. dual-nationals may result in conflicting obligations under the laws of each country. U.S. dual nationals may also face restrictions in the U.S. consular protections available to U.S. nationals abroad, particularly in the country of their other nationality." Notably, the State Department requires dual citizens to use a U.S. passport to enter the country. Does that mean that, when traveling as head of state, Pope Leo has to use a U.S. passport? Unlikely, but intriguing. It strikes me as odd that a person can lead another country and still vote in U.S. elections. With all of those worried about Russian interference in elections, imagine if Vladimir Putin could actually vote in U.S. elections. Obviously, Pope Leo is greatly loved and represents someone whose values are aligned with this country. Yet, he is also the head of state of a foreign nation. SUPREME COURT RULES ON MAIL-IN BALLOTS RECEIVED AFTER ELECTION DAY Under the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA), military personnel and citizens abroad are allowed to vote in U.S. elections. It is no longer considered an absentee vote requiring an excuse but simply a mail-in ballot. The question is whether this right should be suspended when you assume a position in a foreign nation, let alone the head of such a nation. Dual citizenship has long been debated over the difficult questions raised by nations with opposing values and interests. However, being the head of a foreign government with potentially opposing interests and actions to the United States creates a curious status. STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS It turns out that when Gov. Pritzker met with the pope last year, he was actually meeting with a constituent and voter. I am most surprised that the Vatican does not have a policy against such voting, though this is admittedly unprecedented. I would think that the head of the Catholic faith and the head of a foreign government would have a single national citizenship running to the Holy See. All popes are selected from the global faithful by the College of Cardinals and thus have national citizenship with other countries. In assuming their positions, the cardinals "pledge and swear, as individuals and as a group, to observe faithfully and scrupulously the prescriptions contained in the Apostolic Constitution." They also reaffirm that they are not subject to countervailing allegiances or pressures from outside the College: "And never to lend support or favour to any interference, opposition or any other form of intervention, whereby secular authorities of whatever order and degree or any group of people or individuals might wish to intervene in the election of the Roman Pontiff." However, it is fascinating that, once elected, popes do not shed that status upon assuming the head of the Holy See. It is an uncomfortable question since it also raises whether the head of a foreign government should have dual citizenship. Most people were legitimately thrilled, including myself, by the first American pope and can view this as an unlikely "one-off." However, it could just as easily happen with another nation and a dual citizen. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP At the risk of my own excommunication, it seems a worthy question for discussion, even though I doubt any politicians would relish such a debate. For his part, Pope Leo stated before the Villanova-Notre Dame game that the pope will not take sides in the U.S. elections, but Robert Prevost will.

articles.title: Democrats criticize Turek over ad on trans issues
articles.summary: Some Democrats are criticizing Iowa Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek over his recent ad on transgender sports and gender affirming care. “As a kid in a wheelchair, I faced my share of bullying. That’s why I believe that no Iowan should face discrimination. As a Paralympian, I also know it’s important to have rules,” Turek…
articles.body:
Some Democrats are criticizing Iowa Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek over his recent ad on transgender sports and gender affirming care.

“As a kid in a wheelchair, I faced my share of bullying. That’s why I believe that no Iowan should face discrimination. As a Paralympian, I also know it’s important to have rules,” Turek says in the ad.

“It’s why I oppose males competing in female sports, something that is already illegal in Iowa. I’m against taxpayers paying for sex changes too. Anyone tells you any different, is lying,” he adds.

According to a Saturday report from The Washington Post , Osceola County Democratic Party Chair Kathy Winter said Turek’s position was against the platform of the Iowa Democratic Party, which does not support limits for transgender health care.

“At a time of unprecedented hate and bigotry being directed at transgender Iowans, I cannot in good [conscience] vote for a man who is promising to make their lives worse,” Winter said, per a Friday statement obtained by the Post.

In a recent interview with local outlet KCRG, Iowa state Rep. Aime Wichtendahl (D) responded to Turek’s ad by saying that “you don’t need to throw people under the bus to win elections.”

“The plain fact is that these talking points don’t win elections. These talking points aren’t going to gain you anything with the voters,” she added.

Turek’s ad comes after the Republicans and Elon Musk spent millions on ads that falsely targeted his stance on the issue, according to The New York Times . When asked about the ad, the Democrat told CNN’s Manu Raju that he has spoken about the issue many times and that his experience as a Paralympian gives him “more credibility to talk about this than almost any other politician in the country.”

“They’re putting $20 million in negative television ads to try to make me appear somebody I’m not, so I thought it was important we set the record straight,” he said.

“I believe biological males should not compete in female sports, and if that rubs some people in my party the wrong way, we’re a big party, and you don’t have to agree with me on everything,” he added.

In recent years, the issue of transgender rights has become extremely contentious in the U.S. Those on the right have sought to restrict transgender participation in sports categories aligned with people’s gender identity and access to gender affirming care.

During his first day back in office, President Trump signed a sweeping executive order recognizing only two sexes, male and female. The order also directed federal agencies to stop promotion of the concept of gender transition.

articles.title: Lawfare against Elon Musk could affect the Artemis program
articles.summary: Such a move could have profound effects on American space policy and politics.
articles.body:
If the Democrats win one or both houses of Congress, Politico is reporting that on top of their agenda is to wage lawfare against Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla and the world’s richest man. The gavels are warming up for a myriad of investigations into Musk and his businesses. Such a move could have profound effects on American space policy and politics, particularly the Artemis return to the moon program.

SpaceX is one of the businesses that the Democrats would like to delve into. Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), a ranking member of the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee, claims that the “The sheer number of conflicts of interest are astounding.”

The problem is that the next two years are going to be crucial for the Artemis return to the moon program. Artemis III, which will test the two Human Landing Systems, including the SpaceX Starship, is scheduled for 2027. The first moon landing is slated for the following year, 2028. NASA recently revealed the latest progress toward accomplishing that feat.

In the meantime, the Starship is slated for a series of tests that will lead to it becoming an operational vehicle which, among other tasks, will land the first astronauts on the lunar surface since Apollo 17 in 1972.

What a Democratic-controlled Congress might do to place the next moon landing in peril due to its expressed anger at Musk is a matter of speculation. Recently, Bulwark podcaster Kara Swisher suggested that Democrats might actually try to put Musk in jail. Some have even proposed nationalizing SpaceX . It is like a plot line from an Ayn Rand novel.

Even if Democrats hang back from some of the most extreme lawfare tactics against Musk, they can eat up time he might better spend running his companies byy forcing him to attend committee hearing after committee hearing to answer their charges. Musk is a very hands-on manager, and his absence would slow progress on projects ranging from his space-based data centers to getting the Starship ready for lunar landings.

NASA also has the Blue Origin Human Landing System as an option for the Artemis IV moon landing mission. But recent experience with the commercial crew program suggests that two options are better than one where flight hardware is concerned.

Congressional Democrats might want to rethink their plans to wage lawfare on Musk for a variety of reasons. The primary reason is that the Artemis program enjoys wide bipartisan support. Any delays in that program caused by attempts at political retribution risk having the Chinese steal a march on NASA and its international and commercial allies and accomplishing the first moon landing in more than 50 years. The political ramifications would be beyond evaluation, especially if congressional Democrats are to blame.

While Musk has his detractors, as any glance at social media posts would reveal, he remains to many to be the coolest capitalist of them all, purveyor of rocket ships, electric cars and the hope of curing blindness and paralysis with his Neuralink technology. Persecuting such a man risks a backlash.

Also, Musk himself has vowed to fight, warning , “Live by the sword, die by the sword.” Such a warning from a man with Musk’s power, money and influence should not be taken lightly. His pouring of unprecedented amounts of money into midterm campaigns could be seen as the opening shot of such a retaliation

Musk also enjoys the friendship of President Trump, the most powerful man in the world, who is also not afraid of using power and has vowed to use it to defend the SpaceX CEO

If congressional Democrats win back control of one or both houses of Congress (or even if they don’t), they might want to consider doing one of the hardest things to do in politics: take an enemy and make him a friend.

Musk was once a friend and ally of President Barack Obama. Now he sits at Trump’s right hand. Something must have happened to cause this. Democrats should delve into that question and find a way to win Musk back or at least make him apolitical. The effort could be more fruitful than trying to put Musk into prison.

Then sometime in 2028, every American — Republican, Democrat and independent — will be able to bask in the triumph of Americans walking on the moon once again, knowing that a Musk unfettered by subpoenas had much to do with it.

Mark R. Whittington, who writes frequently about space policy, has published a political study of space exploration entitled “ Why is It So Hard to Go Back to the Moon? ” as well a s “ The Moon, Mars and Beyond ” and, most recently, “ Why is America Going Back to the Moon? ” He blogs at Curmudgeons Corner.

articles.title: Trump's DOJ makeover hasn't changed where the political cash is flowing — and the gap is growing
articles.summary: Over 75% of Department of Justice employee donations still go to Democratic committees despite Trump administration efforts to root out partisan bias.
articles.body: The Trump administration has sought to eliminate what it alleges is partisan bias within the Justice Department, but the vast majority of political donations from individuals identifying themselves as DOJ employees are still going to Democratic-aligned committees, according to a Fox News Digital analysis of federal campaign finance records. Between January 2025 and August of this year, just over 75% of campaign contributions from individuals identifying themselves as Department of Justice employees went to Democratic committees, the analysis of federal campaign finance records found. Fox News Digital analyzed roughly $300,000 in political contributions recorded by the Federal Election Commission between January 2025 and August 2026 from donors who listed their employer as "Department of Justice," "DOJ" or a variation of those names. Contributions were categorized by the political affiliation of the recipient candidate or committee, while independent-expenditure committees were classified according to the candidates or parties they supported. When exporting data from the Federal Election Commission's dashboard, an option to include donations from "unique individuals only" was selected to filter out duplicative records. As the Trump administration has progressed, the partisan slant of DOJ donations has become more pronounced. Through 2025, about 70% of donations from those identifying themselves as DOJ staff went to Democratic committees, a figure that rose to just under 90% in 2026, according to Fox News Digital's findings. TODD BLANCHE EXPOSES HOW AGGRESSIVE BIDEN DOJ TARGETED LOW-LEVEL MAR-A-LAGO EMPLOYEES Attorney General Todd Blanche and his predecessor, Pam Bondi, both claimed that the Trump administration inherited a deeply corrupt DOJ, pointing to allegations that the agency was inundated with political bias under President Joe Biden's tenure. "There are a lot of people in the FBI and also in the Department of Justice who despise Donald Trump, despise us," Bondi said in early 2025. "Right now, we’re going to root them out; we will find them, and they will no longer be employed." Critics have pushed back against claims of political weaponization during the Biden administration, arguing that high-profile investigations into President Donald Trump and other conservatives originated from legitimate legal concerns. DOJ DANGLES MASSIVE SIGNING BONUSES FOR LAWYERS READY TO FIGHT ‘LAWLESS’ CITIES FAR BEYOND DC Both of Trump’s attorneys general under his second administration have made strides to recruit a greater number of ideologically aligned lawyers while attempting to push those out who may not be willing to advance the administration’s interests. In early February 2026, DOJ chief of staff Chad Mizelle publicly encouraged lawyers who "support President Trump" to contact him about becoming federal prosecutors. Stephen Miller amplified the appeal on social media with the caption "patriots needed," and sitting U.S. Attorney Jason Quiñones reposted the appeal alongside the phrase "we are hiring!" Mizelle later defended the approach as ensuring that executive-branch lawyers were in line with the elected president’s agenda. LEGAL WAR ON TRUMP’S AGENDA GAINS FIREPOWER AS FEDERAL LAWYERS DEFECT TO DEMOCRATS The administration's personnel overhaul has coincided with a substantial exodus of attorneys from federal service. Over 10,000 attorneys have left federal service since Trump took office for a second term. Fox News Digital reported in July that well over 100 federal attorneys had left the Trump administration for roles in Democratic-run state attorneys general offices. Many of these lawyers took decades of experience with them, prompting concerns that the Trump administration could be depriving itself of the ability to handle highly technical legal matters. Some of these seasoned former federal lawyers have since joined legal action against the Trump administration. While a significant number of government lawyers have left federal service under Trump, and some prominent conservatives have joined the administration, campaign finance records show that Democratic committees continue to receive the overwhelming majority of political contributions from donors identifying themselves as Justice Department employees. Among the most common recipients of donations from those identifying themselves as DOJ employees were Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Emily’s List, a pro-abortion group associated with the Democratic Party. Some conservative committees, such as those in Trump’s network of PACs, were also common targets for Justice Department donors. DEMOCRAT POLITICOS RERUN UNDERHANDED LEFTIST PLAYBOOK IN EFFORT TO TORPEDO TRUMP’S AG NOMINEE Much of the DOJ's work concerns investigations and prosecutions unrelated to partisan politics, and the campaign finance records do not establish whether employees' political preferences have influenced the department's day-to-day operations. Progressive critics, to the contrary, have alleged that the Trump administration is using the Justice Department to target its political enemies. "Those who were fired from the Department were fired for a reason. Those who resigned or took the fork in the road option likely aligned more with the priorities of President Biden and would naturally leave, which is common during transitions," a DOJ spokeswoman previously told Fox News Digital. "The administration gave career employees the fork in the road option to intentionally reduce the size of the government and eliminate unnecessary layers of staff who don’t effectively contribute to the mission of aggressively tackling crime." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The DOJ did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

articles.title: Judge dismisses Trump’s defamation suit against WSJ a second time
articles.summary: A federal judge on Saturday dismissed for the second time President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal in connection with an article about a letter sent to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Last year, the president filed a lawsuit against the Journal after it published an article detailing a 2003 letter he allegedly sent to…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Saturday dismissed for the second time President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal in connection with an article about a letter sent to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Last year, the president filed a lawsuit against the Journal after it published an article detailing a 2003 letter he allegedly sent to Epstein for his 50th birthday. Trump has denied writing the letter and claimed it was fake. In April, a federal judge tossed the lawsuit , ruling that the president failed to establish “actual malice” in his complaint against the outlet.

Following the ruling, Trump filed an amended complaint in May, where his lawyers again argued that he suffered “overwhelming” financial and reputational harm because of the article and said it was filed with “false, defamatory, and malicious statements.”

In Saturday’s ruling , U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles noted that the amended complaint “falls short of pleading actual malice.”

“As President Trump has not plausibly alleged that each Defendant made defamatory statements with actual malice, the Amended Complaint must be dismissed,” the ruling read.

“And because this is President Trump’s second attempt to allege his claims, the Court finds that dismissal with prejudice is appropriate,” it added.

A spokesman for Trump’s legal team told The Hill in a statement that the president “will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants.”

“The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions,” the statement continued.

The letter tied to the Journal’s report was released by the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, which contained a line saying, “Happy Birthday, may every day be another wonderful secret,” inside of a drawing that resembles the silhouette of a woman.

“Of the two surviving individuals who could substantiate whether President Trump had submitted a birthday letter, one person, President Trump, vehemently denied the existence of the alleged letter, and the other person has testified to a federal official that she had no knowledge of it,” the amended complaint filed in May read. The woman referenced in the statement is Epstein’s co-defendant, Ghislaine Maxwell.

“Defendants Safdar, Palazzolo, Dow Jones, and News Corp either knew these facts, or deliberately avoided investigating such information, while nevertheless publishing the false, malicious, and defamatory Article,” it adds.

The latest ruling the judge said that “President Trump’s focus on Maxwell is entirely misplaced,” adding it is not sufficient to plead actual malice.

articles.title: Data analysts flag mismatches in Trump administration California voter eligibility list
articles.summary: Data analysts have flagged mismatches on a Trump administration list concerning California voters’ eligibility and their citizenship status, according to The Associated Press. The outlet reported that over 40 percent of names that the Trump administration labeled as potential California voters who are not U.S. citizens were not on Golden State voter rolls, a Saturday…
articles.body:
Data analysts have flagged mismatches on a Trump administration list concerning California voters’ eligibility and their citizenship status, according to The Associated Press.

The outlet reported that over 40 percent of names that the Trump administration labeled as potential California voters who are not U.S. citizens were not on Golden State voter rolls, a Saturday legal filing from an immigrants’ rights group said.

Per the AP, the outside analysis — done by two University of California, Los Angeles data analysts — on the list was the first of its kind. The Department of Justice (DOJ) has used the list in warning election officials of prosecution. According to the analysis, the list seemingly targeted thousands of U.S. citizens, stating they did not have eligibility to vote.

On Wednesday, the Trump administration’s attempt to section off 20,000 mail ballots in California it said were likely those of noncitizens was dealt another blow, with a trial judge refusing to get involved.

U.S. District Judge David Carter ruled the Golden State could continue to allow the ballots like any other.

“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote.

“If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process,” he continued. “Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.”

California has been skeptical about the validity of the administration’s list and claimed it is not obliged to verify voters’ citizenship.

The Hill has reached out to the Department of Justice for comment.

articles.title: Sen. Tim Scott dodges on whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., declined to say whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race if Democrat Mary Peltola wins the battleground seat
articles.body: Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., declined to say whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race if Democrat Mary Peltola wins following a bombshell report from The New York Times about Democrats’ alleged efforts to recruit a candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent. Asked on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” whether he would accept the election results if Peltola is certified to have won the Senate seat, Scott did not directly answer the question. “Dan Sullivan is going to win, Kristen,” he told moderator Kristen Welker. “You know that, and that’s the only thing I’m going to tell you because it’s the truth.” Scott went on to criticize Democrats for allegedly working to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, a controversy that exploded last week following a report from The New York Times. “What I can tell you about the truth is you can’t trust Mary Peltola’s campaign and the collusion between her campaign and the DSCC,” said Scott, who also serves as the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP counterpart to the DSCC. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Democrats allegedly sought to recruit a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan. The report said the efforts allegedly involved members of the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which works to elect Democrats to the Senate. Following the report, the DSCC said in a statement that it “is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.” Peltola, too, said she “knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent.” Asked a second time whether he would accept the election results, Scott dodged the question. “Number one, Dan Sullivan, the real Dan Sullivan, will win,” said Scott. “And number two, it actually is a federal offense to confuse voters.” NBC News has previously reported that people who worked to recruit the challenger Dan J. Sullivan did not necessarily violate the law. Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who was fired in August, participated in interviews with The New York Times, but later said she retracted “all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate race.” Before The New York Times report was published, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit in Alaska seeking to block the certification of the results of the Senate election if Dan S. Sullivan loses. The DOJ cited potential voter confusion over having another candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. In the aftermath of the Times’ report, President Donald Trump has said that both Peltola and the challenger Sullivan should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. On Thursday, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was ordering a state investigation to determine whether the alleged “scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted.”

articles.title: Sullivan: ‘I’m going to accept the election results’
articles.summary: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) said he would accept the election results of the upcoming 2026 elections, even if he lost, following a Justice Department (DOJ) lawsuit attempting to invalidate election results if his opponent, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska), won. Appearing on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Sullivan was asked by host Jake Tapper if…
articles.body:
Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) said he would accept the election results of the upcoming 2026 elections, even if he lost, following a Justice Department (DOJ) lawsuit attempting to invalidate election results if his opponent, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska), won.

Appearing on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Sullivan was asked by host Jake Tapper if he would only accept the election results if he won.

“No, I‘m going to accept the election results,” Sullivan said.

The senator has hammered Peltola recently over a New York Times report that alleged her campaign and national Democrats “ballot-stacked” the Alaska Senate race by recruiting another candidate who shared the same name as Sullivan.

In his appearance, the senator accused Peltola of being “directly involved” in the scheme and continued that certain federal statues “would maybe make this about not being legal at all.”

The DOJ had previously sued to block certification of the Alaska Senate race if Sullivan loses, a move which legal and election experts said had no basis in court.

President Trump similarly said he would respect the result of Tuesday’s midterm results “ if they’re honest elections ,” after calling for Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan to be removed from Alaskan ballots.

While Peltola, her campaign and national Democrats denied the allegations, other federal authorities alongside the House Oversight Committee have launched separate probes into the matter.

U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael Heyman said that the investigation has been in the works for several months but that federal authorities are looking into the matter “intensely and swiftly” after “troubling new revelations” were reported by The Times.

Oversight Committee Chair James Comer (R-Ky.) also already sent letters to both Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who The Times spoke with, and Jerid Kurtz, a Democratic operative, requesting in-person, transcribed interviews.

He requested that Rios testify on Nov. 5 and Kurtz on Nov. 6.

articles.title: Trump slams ex-lawyer’s $50m deal with pardoned banker’s family
articles.summary: Alina Habba Mildon signed lucrative contract while working at the Justice Department, before Trump pardoned the banker.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has criticised one of his former lawyers for signing a contract worth more than $50 million with the family of a Venezuelan banker whom Trump later pardoned.

Alina Habba Mildon reportedly signed the lucrative deal while working as a federal prosecutor and later began working for the banker’s family while still being employed as an adviser to the US Department of Justice.

“I thought it was totally obnoxious and outrageous, and it’s not acceptable,” Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Saturday.

According to The New York Times, Habba Mildon signed a four-year contract in October 2025 with a company owned by the family of Julio Herrera Velutini, a Venezuelan banker who was seeking a presidential pardon.

Herrera was accused of bribing former Puerto Rico Governor Wanda Vazquez Garced in exchange for removing a financial regulator who was investigating his bank. He was facing federal bribery charges in the US before reaching a plea deal with prosecutors in August 2025.

Habba Mildon’s contract with his family’s company guaranteed her more than $50 million over four years, including an annual salary of $10 million and bonuses.

When she signed the deal, Habba Mildon was the acting US attorney for New Jersey, a position Trump had appointed her to after working as his personal lawyer.

She left that position in December after a court ruled she could not legally serve in the role. She then immediately took another job at the Justice Department as a senior adviser to the attorney general.

On January 1 , Habba Mildon officially began working for the banker’s family while still employed by the Justice Department.

Two weeks later, on January 15 , Trump granted Herrera a full presidential pardon.

The arrangement has raised questions about potential conflicts of interest, given Habba Mildon’s government position and her ties to Trump.

The company that hired her, Concord Partners, has no public profile and its business activities remain unclear, according to The New York Times.

Habba Mildon has denied having any role in securing Herrera’s pardon.

Last week, she said she had never been paid to obtain a pardon, had never discussed one with anyone at the White House or the Justice Department and had never worked to secure a pardon for anyone.

Trump was reportedly furious when he learned about the size of her contract.

The New York Times reported that he told aides and allies that Habba Mildon should donate some of the money to his future presidential library or another Trump-related organisation.

He also reportedly told at least one ally that Herrera’s family should stop paying her the remainder of the contract.

Speaking on Saturday, Trump said he told Habba Mildon he did not want her to be paid, describing the situation as “terrible”.

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

articles.title: Why you can’t wear, bring political gear to a polling place in these states
articles.summary: States have different guidance regarding electioneering at or near a polling place.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Regardless of the campaign signs in your yard or how much you support a candidate, any outward support of that person or party may throw a wrench in your plans to vote for them.

More than half of U.S. states do not allow voters to wear campaign apparel while casting their ballot, while nearly all prohibit signs, banners, or literature near the polling place, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures .

These restrictions have caused a stir before, specifically in 2024 when then-vice presidential candidate JD Vance weighed in on a photo of a bra-clad woman purportedly voting shirtless after a poll worker told her the Trump campaign shirt she was wearing violated electioneering prohibitions. The woman opted to take the shirt off after firing multiple expletives at the worker.

Electioneering rules are meant to keep people from feeling pressured or intimidated in any way while voting, said Quinn Yeargain, an associate professor of law at Michigan State University.

“This is not something that functions in any way to chill anybody’s free speech,” Yeargain said. “This is to keep polling places neutral locations.”

Twenty-seven states have rules against campaign wearables, like stickers, shirts, and buttons, according to the NCSL.

Voters wearing “candidate paraphernalia” at Vermont polling places will need to cover it, officials warn. Michigan , Minnesota , and Texas have similar prohibitions.

“The polling place is about voting, not campaigning – once voters have entered the polling place the campaigns have ended,” Vermont officials said.

In Colorado , Louisiana , and Nebraska , voters can’t wear anything regarding a candidate or a ballot measure that they’re voting on. Voters in Delaware , Georgia , and Oklahoma cannot wear items supporting a candidate while at a polling place.

Other states that prohibit voters from wearing campaign shirts, buttons, or other gear include Arkansas, California, Hawaii, Indiana, Kansas, Maine (small buttons are allowed), Massachusetts, Montana, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Rhode Island, South Carolina, and Tennessee, according to NCSL.

Maryland and Iowa allow voters to wear buttons or clothing related to a campaign, but they must leave “immediately after voting.” New Hampshire voters who “cannot reasonably” remove or cover “clothing with electioneering messages on it” are allowed to “expeditiously [register] to vote or [vote].”

Alabama voters are similarly advised not to loiter or leave campaign materials at the polling place, while Pennsylvania voters are not allowed to “campaign for or encourage others to support a candidate” inside. Voters, and only voters, in Virginia can wear campaign apparel, but election workers cannot.

Nearly every state prohibits campaigning and electioneering within a certain proximity of the polling place.

In Massachusetts , for example, “electioneering, campaigning, signature-gathering and other specific political activities intended to influence the current election” is not allowed within 150 feet of the polling location. Georgia also prohibits campaigning within 150 feet of a polling site.

In Nebraska , the restriction begins at 200 feet, while Idaho law mandates a limit at 250 feet. In Oklahoma , it’s 300 feet, and in South Carolina , some restrictions begin within 500 feet of a polling site. In Louisiana , it’s 600 feet.

It’s even shorter in Pennsylvania – “at least 10 feet from the voting-room entrance” – and Alabama , where the law says campaigning cannot happen within 30 feet of the entrance.

Lines are established at Maryland polling places “as near as practicable to 100 feet” from the entrance for electioneering. In Colorado , there is no campaigning allowed within 100 feet of any polling location or ballot drop-box. Minnesota , Texas , and West Virginia also prohibit electioneering within 100 feet of a polling place.

New Hampshire law calls for “no-electioneering corridors” of at least 10 feet in width that stretch “from all entrances of the polling place a reasonable distance along the sidewalks or to the parking lots that serve the polling place.”

Before you head out to the polls, it’s best to confirm what campaigning, if any, is permitted in or near your polling place.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Democratic rival, Haley Stevens, endorses GOP's Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
articles.summary: DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republ...
articles.body:
DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers after Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.

Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.

"Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."

Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.

Democrats had hoped that Sunday would be a show of unity. Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.

The latest and late-stage infighting comes as Democrats look to drive turnout among Black and Jewish voters in key strongholds. El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is in a tight race with Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by Democrat Gary Peters, who is retiring. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party's effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump's second term.

Stevens' team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal

Plans for Stevens to join El-Sayed and Clyburn unraveled after a dispute over Israel and an outside group's campaign advertisement escalated into a public exchange of criticism between the rivals.

After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, "I'm not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote."

Rogers, standing beside her, said he was "honored" by her support.

Their appearance stunned Democrats, coming days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for the nominee, and led her longtime chief of staff to resign with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.

"We are shocked and heartbroken," the aide said in a statement.

The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens' endorsement "shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about."

"We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us," Hertel wrote.

Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began.

El-Sayed spoke for nearly 10 minutes at the service. He did not address the latest controversy.

"It's in churches like this, in pews like the ones in which you sit, that the foundation of my life was built," El-Sayed said.

Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became 'distracting'

Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance in hopes of bringing together Democrats in the final days before Tuesday's vote, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that.

"I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," Dingell said in a telephone interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. "This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank."

Dingell and other Democrats insist the party is united behind El-Sayed. Early voting has been underway since Oct. 24, before the latest tensions resurfaced, complicating efforts to deliver a unified closing message in crucial areas such as Detroit, where turnout could prove decisive.

Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County, in the primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition.

The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee's affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group's ad accusing him of disrespecting women.

Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his summer win.

Last week Stevens' fiancé told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Stevens later appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to "shut out the hate and call it out."

But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.

"Abdul promises to get money out of politics," Stevens wrote. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."

El-Sayed responded: "So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let's all focus on the task at hand."

He made clear the ad was not made by his campaign and "I do not agree with the contents of that ad."

articles.title: Trump calls Alina Habba Mildon’s $50M deal ‘obnoxious’
articles.summary: President Trump called his former lawyer Alina Habba Mildon’s alleged $50 million deal for a presidential pardon “obnoxious and outrageous.” While at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago in Florida, Trump had some harsh words for Habba Mildon, who was accused in a recent New York Times report of accepting a deal worth $50 million from…
articles.body:
President Trump called his former lawyer Alina Habba Mildon’s alleged $50 million deal for a presidential pardon “obnoxious and outrageous.”

While at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago in Florida, Trump had some harsh words for Habba Mildon, who was accused in a recent New York Times report of accepting a deal worth $50 million from Venezuelan billionaire Julio Herrera Velutini.

The deal intended for Habba Mildon to work to secure a presidential pardon in her capacity as a senior advisor at the Justice Department.

“I thought it was terrible. I told her,” Trump told reporters. “I said I don’t want her paid. I thought we had somebody speak to the people that did it, and she used her relationship to do that.”

“And it was far too much. You know, it’s one thing for a person to get paid legal fees or whatever, she’s a lawyer. I thought it was totally obnoxious and outrageous, and it’s not acceptable. Not acceptable,” the president continued.

A reporter followed up with Trump on reports that he told White House aides that Mildon should donate a portion of the $50 million to the president’s future presidential library or another Trump business, per The Times.

“Not [Habba]. I expect many people. I don’t know if anybody wants to make it, but it’s unacceptable what she did. Unacceptable,” he responded.

The contract Mildon accepted reportedly guaranteed her $10 million a year for four years alongside bonuses, according to interviews and documents obtained by The Times, which stated her work started in January weeks before Trump gave Herrera a full pardon for misdemeanor campaign finance violations.

Herrera, the founder of Bancrédito International Bank & Trust, also faced charges in 2022 for conspiracy, bribery and fraud.

articles.title: Trump White House maps path to govern without Congress if Democrats win
articles.summary: By Nandita Bose and Tim Reid WASHINGTON, Nov 1 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover...
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump host a Halloween event at the White House

WASHINGTON, Nov 1 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, developing plans to keep advancing major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing for investigations of his administration, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the plans.

Senior officials, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director ‌Russell Vought, have been working with the White House Counsel's Office since April to identify executive actions on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending that Trump could pursue without congressional approval, said the three people, who ‌spoke on the condition of anonymity.

White House counsel Will Scharf and his team also are looking at "what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court," the White House official said.

The planning underscores a paradox of Tuesday's ​midterm elections: Capturing control of Congress would give Democrats the power to investigate Trump, block legislation and constrain his spending priorities. But Trump would retain broad executive authority over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy that he has already used aggressively during his second term.

If Republicans lose control of Congress, Trump said he expects he could issue vetoes for "a month or two" before reaching compromises with Democrats.

"I guess I'll become Mr. Veto," Trump told the New York Post's Pod Force One podcast in an interview excerpt released on Sunday. "And then at some point, we'll probably make deals."

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the US Senate to overturn Republicans' narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities. Opinion polls favor Democrats to win the House, ‌while the Senate remains too close to call.

For the past month, Trump has held rallies ⁠across the country trying to preserve Republican control of Congress, even as his aides privately prepare for a very different political landscape in 2027.

The White House pushed back on the prospect of Republican losses and accused the media of promoting a false narrative.

"This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of ⁠hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

Among the executive actions under consideration are new tariffs on imports of critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter rules on visas for international students and temporary foreign workers, and measures aimed at lowering housing and construction costs, the White House official said.

Federal agencies have submitted proposals and legal reviews of actions the administration could take unilaterally, one of the people with knowledge of the plans said.

Vought, whose US Office of Management and Budget oversees federal spending, is examining which priorities can ​move ​forward using money already appropriated by Congress, two of the people said.

He also wants to change federal grant rules to give political appointees ​more say in which government programs receive taxpayer money, they said, potentially giving the White House ‌more influence over federal spending without seeking congressional approval.

Trump has been briefed on the preparations and has taken part in discussions about them, the White House official said.

When asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive authority under a Democratic Congress, one of the people said, "very comfortable."

Trump has already tested the reach of presidential power since returning to office in January 2025, using executive authority to impose sweeping tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, shrink the federal workforce, and pursue foreign-policy goals including the war against Iran without Congress' approval or new laws.

A major exception was Trump's massive package of tax and spending cuts that was passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the president in July 2025.

"President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power," said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides nonpartisan political analysis. "I think he will only continue if there are Democratic majorities."

Trump has repeatedly invoked ‌national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation. Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such ​a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him.

A Democratic Congress could still create significant obstacles.

Control of the Senate would allow Democrats to ​block Trump's judicial and executive-branch nominees, including any Supreme Court pick.

"I would anticipate they will be very reluctant to ​approve any of the president's appointments," said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.

Democrats could also refuse to pass Trump-backed ‌legislation. But Trump could veto Democratic legislation he doesn't like, and Democrats are unlikely to ​have enough votes in the House to override him.

Courts could block ​executive actions that exceed Trump's legal authority. The White House plans to seek legal opinions from the Justice Department to determine what Trump can do without Congress and how to defend those actions if they are challenged in court, one of the people said.

One challenge, however, cannot be sidestepped through executive action: congressional investigations.

Reuters previously reported that senior House Democrats and committee aides have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document requests to examine whether Trump has used ​his presidential power to benefit himself, allies or donors.

Trump aides have been preparing for that ‌prospect for months, all three people said.

White House lawyers have been briefing political appointees and agency leaders on how to handle congressional inquiries, document requests and subpoenas, one person said. They have advised officials to ​be careful about what they put in writing.

They also sought a Justice Department opinion that could allow Trump to invoke executive privilege to shield communications with private advisers from congressional scrutiny, the person said.

(Reporting by ​Nandita Bose and Tim Reid, additional reporting by Doina Chiacu; Editing by Colleen Jenkins, Alistair Bell, Will Dunham and Sergio Non)

articles.title: Trump rallies in Iowa, Kansas to maintain Republican control of US Senate
articles.summary: US President Trump returns to the campaign trail after taking a break at his ⁠⁠Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Saturday.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump is set to rally in Iowa and Kansas, two Republican-leaning states he previously won, in a bid to maintain Republican control of the United States Senate.

His first stop is Sunday afternoon in Dubuque, Iowa, where Republicans are battling to retain a critical Senate seat and the governorship. Trump won Iowa by double digits in 2024.

The 2nd Congressional District, which includes Dubuque, has also become competitive as the GOP works to protect its fragile majority in the US House of Representatives. The battle is on between Gen Z Republican candidate Joe Mitchell and Democrat Lindsay James.

On Sunday, Trump also plans to visit Salina, Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932 but now faces an unexpectedly ⁠⁠close race between incumbent Republican Roger Marshall and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, a prominent pastor.

The trips mark Trump’s return to the campaign trail after taking a break at his ⁠⁠Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Saturday. He has spent weeks campaigning across multiple US states.

Republicans abruptly cancelled the Iowa and Kansas stops late Thursday, only to reschedule them. A source close to the Trump administration told Al Jazeera on Friday that Trump will be headlining the previously cancelled rallies in person.

“Rallies are BACK ON!” the source said. “No one works harder, fights harder, or loves the American people more than President Donald J. Trump!”

Polls show Democrats tied with or leading Republicans in many of the states’ races, and Trump’s approval among rural Americans fell to a new low of 45 percent in October, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.

In this campaign, Trump has focused largely on states he has dominated before as voters, including previous supporters, question the economic fallout of his decision to impose tariffs and launch the war in Iran.

Thirty-five Senate seats and all 435 House seats are on the ballot on Tuesday . Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House. Losing either chamber would let Democrats block Trump’s agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities.

More than 52 million Americans have already voted in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, a record for a midterm and up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day in 2022.

articles.title: Tim Scott dodges question on accepting Alaska Senate race results if Peltola wins
articles.summary: Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) on Sunday dodged whether he would accept the Alaska Senate election results in the case that Democrat Mary Peltola is victorious in the race against incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). During an interview on NBC News’s “Meet the Press,” Kristen Welker asked the Palmetto State senator on possibly accepting the Alaska…
articles.body:
Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) on Sunday dodged whether he would accept the Alaska Senate election results in the case that Democrat Mary Peltola is victorious in the race against incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska).

During an interview on NBC News’s “Meet the Press,” Kristen Welker asked the Palmetto State senator on possibly accepting the Alaska Senate results. Scott did not give a straightforward answer when Welker questioned him initially, so she pressed him again.

“Just to go back to my original question, senator. If Mary Peltola wins, if the election is certified, will you accept the results of that race?” Welker asked.

“Kristen, two things: Number one, Dan Sullivan, the real Dan S. Sullivan, will win, and number two, it actually is a federal offense to confuse voters, that’s the law, and that’s why you’ve seen the Department of Justice ask for — send out 30 subpoenas,” Scott responded, referencing the Department of Justice (DOJ) reportedly issuing dozens of subpoenas linked to ballot-stacking allegations against Peltola.

“So, what we’re going to find out very quickly is who all was involved in this attempt to confuse the voters. It’s okay to expand the ballot, but it is not okay to confuse the voters,” he added.

Last week, The New York Times reported that there was direct involvement from Peltola’s campaign in recruiting a person with the same name as her opponent, the incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. The presence of Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot resulted in the DOJ filing a lawsuit, alleging it gave an unfair boost to Peltola.

The fresh DOJ subpoenas were sent to the Alaska Democrat’s campaign offices, as well as the offices of Daniel J. Sullivan, according to NBC News.

In a Truth Social post last week, President Trump said Peltola should face legal and political consequences.

“It has just been determined that the Democrats in Alaska illegally searched for, and recruited, a man named Dan Sullivan to run against our distinguished Republican Senator, Dan Sullivan, in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election, thereby taking votes away from the REAL Senator, Dan Sullivan,” the president wrote.

Peltola has denied multiple times any involvement in the alleged ballot-stacking plot.

The Hill has reached out to Daniel. J Sullivan and Mary Peltola’s campaigns for comment.
