articles.title: The dangerous illusion of ‘a little Epic Fury’
articles.summary: To get us out of this war, Trump needs to focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and tune out voices advocating for more of the same failed tactics.
articles.body:
As President Trump contemplates a return to kinetic warfare with Iran in the coming days and weeks under what has been dubbed “a little Epic Fury,” it is important to take into account one immutable fact about warfare: The enemy gets a vote.

Trump should trust his well-honed business instincts, not the advisors who got him into this war by promising a quick victory. He should recall that, in June, he correctly assessed the first round of Epic Fury: It left him in a military stalemate and had such a negative effect on the economy that he was close to becoming Herbert Hoover and triggering an economic depression in the U.S.

Because of the economic effects of the war, Trump entered into a memorandum of understanding to stop the fighting and get oil flowing again. This was the right call. The most critical issue was then, and remains now, reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Throughout the initial phase of this conflict, the original Epic Fury, the U.S. expended thousands of munitions against Iranian military sites and inflicted enormous damage on the Iranian economy by striking critical dual-use infrastructure. By some estimates , the bombing damage alone exceeded $100 billion. And yet, despite enormous destruction, decapitation strikes against Iranian leadership and the imposition of a blockade that has lasted more than 100 days , Iran is still standing.

Although the economic situation in Iran is dire, there is very little evidence to suggest that bombing power stations and additional economic and civilian infrastructure will bring about the financial stress, fragmentation and anarchy that eight months of destruction could not.

Since the war began, Iran’s currency has cratered from 1.72 million to 2.7 million to the dollar, representing a 36.3 percent decline in its value. Yet there is little to suggest that Iranian citizens are days away from taking to the streets en masse to overthrow the regime.

In contrast, the American population is overwhelmingly opposed to the Iran War, with Pew Research finding that 65 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the conflict. Rapidly rising energy prices have significantly affected ordinary Americans. With oil trading at $113 per barrel, diesel above $6.00 per gallon and gasoline close to $4.20 per gallon, the economic situation remains serious.

To get us out of this war, Trump needs to focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and tune out voices advocating for more of the same failed tactics that got us into this situation in the first place. Another bombing campaign risks triggering a major economic crisis at home, particularly if Iran responds by targeting additional Gulf energy infrastructure. A return to military operations also risks needlessly getting more American troops killed without a discernible military objective.

Despite an enormous bombing campaign that destroyed much of Iran’s Navy, Air Force and original leadership, strikes against vessels attempting to transit the Omani Route reached an all-time high in October. Iran has also reportedly conducted dozens of missile tests this month, including more than 30 reported on Oct. 11, alone, in preparation for a potential resumption of all-out war.

Nothing currently indicates that Iran lacks the capability to retaliate against further U.S. bombing in ways that could devastate the global economy, particularly after global energy reserves have been depleted throughout eight months of war.

Iran has proven that it cannot simply be bombed into submission and that its leaders are unlikely to give Trump a diplomatic end to the war without major concessions. As this conflict has become existential for the Iranian regime, and repeated efforts to reach a negotiated settlement have failed, more restraint-oriented figures in Tehran are being sidelined by those who believe that only catastrophic damage to the global economy can bring about an end to the war.

Given Iran’s demonstrated ability to strike targets not just in Hormuz, but also in the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Gulf , alongside an increasingly fragile global energy market, the premise of a “little Epic Fury” risks producing an Iranian retaliation that delivers precisely the Herbert Hoover economy Trump sought to avoid.

Returning to the memorandum of understanding or simply declaring victory and walking away are two of the most rational options available to Trump. Returning to the memorandum of understanding would align with the Iranian leadership’s repeated demands and revive an agreement Trump has already accepted.

But if he deems this a bridge too far, he can instead declare victory, lift the blockade and withdraw American forces from the region, thereby substantially reducing Iran’s rationale for threatening shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. This would create opportunities for diplomatic progress while allowing both sides to claim victory in the meantime.

The appeal of giving Iran just one more push is understandable. The damage inflicted by the U.S. has been immense. But Trump cannot assume that he can dictate the duration of another kinetic phase of this war.

Joe Kent is a former director of the United States National Counterterrorism Center. Brett Erickson is managing principal of Obsidian Risk Advisors.

articles.title: Inside top Trump bulldog’s plan to save House GOP majority and defy history
articles.summary: Jim Jordan has barnstormed 115 districts across 34 states this election cycle, raising millions for House Republicans fighting to keep their majority.
articles.body: Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, was jumping into the car with his wife on the way to the airport when he took a call from a Fox News Digital reporter on Thursday morning. It’s a microcosm of what the House Judiciary Committee chairman’s recent weeks and months have been: a seemingly endless series of planes, trains and automobiles across the U.S. campaigning for fellow Republican lawmakers. House Republicans’ senior leadership is crisscrossing the country raising money and support for their members to win Tuesday’s midterm elections. Jordan, though he’s not part of the trio, has much the same schedule. "Sometimes they’re fundraisers, sometimes they’re rallies, sometimes they're both," Jordan said. "We're doing everything we can just to help our team win, because… if these Democrats get in there, my real concern, I gotta be honest, is what they're gonna try to do to the structure of our government." MAPPED: TRUMP’S NONSTOP CAMPAIGN BLITZ SWEEPS KEY STATES A source familiar with Jordan’s travel schedule said he’ll have gone to 115 districts across 34 states during this election cycle. That includes 19 consecutive days on the road in the lead-up to Nov. 3 in states such as Washington, Oregon, Texas, Arkansas, Florida, Illinois and South Carolina. And despite the diverse areas, Jordan said his message is mostly the same: Republicans cut taxes, secured the border and Democrats will make it all worse. "We understand things cost a little too much, and we're working on that. But remember, most of that's because of the Biden administration and their record inflation. We're bringing that inflation rate down, but you know, we still understand things, things cost too much, and we're gonna keep working on that," Jordan said. The Stevens announcement came after days of fueding between the Democrats, and just two days before the midterm elections. Democrats are seeking…
articles.body:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) on Sunday endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) to serve in the Senate over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated her in a bitter primary battle over the summer.

The Stevens announcement came after days of fueding between the Democrats, and just two days before the midterm elections.

Democrats are seeking to hold on to the Michigan Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Gary Peters (D). A loss in Michigan would make it more difficult for the party to win the Senate majority. Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to take the majority.

Anger over Israel and the Gaza war was at the heart of the Stevens-El-Sayed primary fight, their subsequent feud and Stevens’s decision to endorse a Republican.

Stevens had called on El-Sayed to publicly disavow a campaign ad run by an outside group. He refused, and over the weekend, made it clear Stevens was not welcome at a Sunday campaign event where she had been invited through other Democrats seeking to put the messy fight behind the party.

“As you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign, and that I should stay away. And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing my Rogers for the United States Senate today,” Stevens said in a video posted on the social platform X.

Her endorsement came after she appeared at church on Sunday alongside Rogers, a move that enraged Michigan Democrats.

In a Sunday post from Rogers’s campaign staffer Abby Ronson on the social platform X, Stevens is seen in a photo standing next to the GOP nominee, with the caption reading , “HAPPENING NOW: Congresswoman Haley Stevens joins Mike Rogers at church in Detroit this morning.”

“We have a state to save, Michigan,” the post continued.

Michigan Democrats released a statement blasting Rogers and Stevens.

“Mike Rogers is Donald Trump’s hand-picked candidate for Senate, a rubber stamp for Trump’s toxic agenda, and a corrupt politician looking out only for himself,” said Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel.

“The Michigan Democratic Party stands united and fully behind Abdul El-Sayed, a proven, committed fighter for Michigan’s working families. Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers—a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda—shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about,” he continued. “We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us.”

On Friday, El-Sayed, who if elected would be the nation’s first Muslim senator, called out Stevens after she expected him to apologize due to his remarks on Israel only days away from the midterm elections.

Stevens said this weekend she would appear with El-Sayed for the first time since the August primary. But El-Sayed dropped Stevens from the event, according to sources familiar with matter.

“So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics,” El-Sayed said in a statement posted on X.

Stevens had targeted the Democratic nominee because of his response to a controversial ad that appeared to connect Israel to high grocery prices in the U.S. and which some viewed as antisemitic.

El-Sayed has expressed his desire for the U.S. to cut off financial aid to Israel and instead spend that money on domestic issues. During the Democratic primary, Stevens received millions from pro-Israel lobbying groups, a major point of contention between the candidates.

Following her loss, Stevens backed El-Sayed and endorsed him.

However, Stevens’s fiancé, who is Jewish, recently said he would cast his ballot for Rogers.

The tension between El-Sayed and Stevens represents a broader split among Democrats over the issue of support for Israel, with many disapproving of the country’s actions in its war in Gaza, which some have labeled as a “genocide.”

The Hill has reached out to Stevens’s office and El-Sayed’s campaign for further comment.

articles.title: Rep. Haley Stevens endorses GOP candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
articles.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday, a major shake-up in the final stages of a top battleground race that could determine which party controls the Senate.
articles.body: Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday, a major shake-up in the final stages of a top battleground race that could determine which party controls the Senate. “Hey, Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video. “And he’s right, and that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today,” she said. “I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign.” The congresswoman’s announcement marks a whirlwind turnaround from just days ago, when she said she would support her party’s ticket and planned to attend a campaign event on Sunday to support Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. But leading up to the rally, Stevens and El-Sayed released dueling critical public statements, prompting concerns from Democrats that the spat was a distraction from what is widely seen as one of the most competitive Senate races. Stevens had said that she expected El-Sayed to condemn an ad from an outside group that she said was antisemitic. El-Sayed responded, accusing Stevens of being “intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” NBC News reported Saturday that El-Sayed’s campaign had asked Stevens to no longer attend campaign events following the dueling statements. In her endorsement video, which was less than two minutes, Stevens referenced El-Sayed’s ties to Hasan Piker, who has appeared with El-Sayed at campaign events. “I do not stand with Hasan Piker, who gets trafficked on our college campuses,” she said. “A dear friend of mine earlier today was saying that education is the ballot, and she’s absolutely right. And what our students see, what our children see, and who we are as Michiganders is not hate, and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.” Stevens said she was “still a very proud Democrat.” Speaking with reporters shortly after she posted her endorsement, Stevens reiterated that El-Sayed “made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign.” “At some point, you got to look at who’s standing for country,” she added later. NBC News has reached out to El-Sayed’s and Rogers’ campaigns for comment on Stevens’ endorsement. Speaking to reporters after Stevens, Rogers said he was “honored” to have the congresswoman’s support. He said that sometimes “the hate grows so loud that it jeopardizes some of our citizens in this state.” He referenced Jews hiding symbols of their faith and being “harassed for being Jewish.” “This is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else,” Rogers said. “And I just want you to know: She reminded me at the end of the call, ‘Remember, I’m still a Democrat.’” President Donald Trump praised Stevens for her endorsement of Rogers, saying in a Truth Social post that she “showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did.” “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!” he said. Stevens’ announcement came after she appeared alongside Rogers at church in Detroit, Rogers spokesperson Abby Ronson confirmed. “Mike welcomes her,” Ronson told NBC News ahead of Stevens’ endorsement. Stevens’ criticism of El-Sayed, her onetime primary opponent, and appearance alongside Rogers on Sunday have infuriated Democratic allies of El-Sayed, who have spent the weekend responding to Stevens’ criticisms of the party’s candidate in the crucial window before Election Day. Even within her own congressional office, Stevens’ decision to endorse Rogers appeared to have quick ripple effects. A person familiar with the matter confirmed that Stevens’ longtime chief of staff Justin German, as well as several other staff members in her congressional office, are resigning over Stevens’ decision to endorse Rogers. In a statement, German said his team was “shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’ decision to support Mike Rogers.” “As of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself,” he said later in the statement. “We encourage everyone to exercise their civic duty, vote for Abdul and Democrats up and down the ballot, and stand up for the America we all believe in.” Beyond her office, the Democratic National Committee’s Black Caucus Chair Virgie Rollins excoriated Stevens, saying in a statement that the congresswoman “revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt.” “Congresswoman Stevens has lost her way, and Michiganders know that Mike Rogers is a shill for Trump and has failed Michigan,” Rollins said. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary but endorsed El-Sayed after his primary victory, said in a statement that “Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed.” He said that El-Sayed “will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors.” A Democratic operative who has worked in Michigan questioned why more state Democratic leaders were not immediately coming out hard against Stevens’ move. “Ask yourself where is Gretchen Whitmer right now?” this person said. “What is she doing?” Whitmer did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “No one’s quite sure what’s going on here, but the party has basically said, if you’re a surrogate, go on the attack against her [Stevens] right now,” this person added. Still, it’s unclear how much Stevens’ endorsement could affect the race’s outcome. More than 2 million votes have already been cast in the state, according to NBC News data.

articles.title: The polling average won. Now what?
articles.summary: The author argues that while modern polling averages provide immediate insights into election margins, journalists must look deeper into the underlying data to understand voter motivations and mandates.
articles.body:
The polling average won. Twenty years ago, in The Washington Post, I worried that the new fashion for averaging treated every survey as an equal ingredient, and I wrote, “ We need standards, not averages .” Today the averages update by the hour, prediction-market odds move continuously, and a Senate margin can change before lunch. We have a better sense than ever of who is up and who is down, but a diminished sense of why.

We are not better informed about the campaigns. Seventeen percent of Maine voters who disapprove of President Trump plan to vote for Sen. Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent. In a race this close, they could decide who controls the Senate. In 2020, Joe Biden carried Maine by 9 points, and Collins still won by nearly as much. The polls tell us these voters are there. The averages and markets leave their reasons out of the picture. That should be the beginning of an inquiry.

A September New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll had Collins up 3 points, inside the margin of error. Most polls since show the race tied or give Democrat Troy Jackson an edge. The split among her own voters has held: About a third of Collins supporters disapproved of Trump, and only half said they’d rather have a senator who supports him. The tables offer clues: Voters saw her as the more effective senator, and nearly two-thirds of her voters called Jackson too far to the left. In an early-September CNN poll , a majority of Collins voters said their vote wasn’t a message about Trump at all. But no published table shows how Collins voters who disapprove of Trump answered any of these questions. The coverage stops at the margin.

On Nov. 3, some of the estimates will be right, and some will be wrong; we will spend weeks arguing about which. That’s the wrong fight. The real battle is over what the results mean. Who has a mandate, and for what? What kinds of candidates do voters want, and which positions? That debate usually runs on anecdote and spin. It should run on data, and the data exist.

Take data centers. No single poll tells that story. A dozen do. Gallup , Fox News , Emerson , and The Economist/YouGov all found national majorities this year against a data center near home, from 63 to 71 percent; Quinnipiac found 74 percent in Pennsylvania. Heatmap and Embold Research have asked the same question four times since August 2025, and opposition rose from 42 percent to 75 percent. A candidate who wins on that could claim a mandate to stop data centers from being built in their constituents’ backyards. Read the rest of the tables, and the mandate looks different. The common thread is the electric bill.

Pew found Americans who had heard of data centers six times as likely to call them bad for home energy costs as good. Six in 10 told YouGov a nearby one would raise what they pay. And when Echelon Insights asked voters to assume data centers would cover their own grid costs so bills did not rise, 54 percent said local officials should allow them; 34 percent said ban them. Opposition is a headline. Together, these polls suggest a different question for the winners: Would voters accept data centers if developers paid the costs?

Most of those tables are public. AI can search them in seconds. It can bring findings from a dozen polls together and help us see where the answers converge, where they differ, and what no one has asked. AI can also misread a column or mix up two groups. That CNN poll found that 30 percent of Collins voters disapproved of Trump. Turn the question around, and 20 percent of Trump disapprovers supported Collins. Both are true. Confuse the denominators, and you will tell the wrong story.

So the rules I asked for in 2006 still apply: disclosure from pollsters, judgment from newsrooms. When AI turns up an interesting number, a reporter should be able to see the exact question, who answered it, and where it appears in the tables. If any of that is missing, the number isn’t ready for print. If it checks out, use it to write the next question. Recontact willing respondents, or draw a fresh sample with enough of these cross-pressured voters to hear them out. Let them explain, in their own words, why they vote the way they do and what could change their minds. A campaign teaches us things. Our questionnaires should learn, too.

I was too neat in 2006. Good averages have earned their place. But they were never built to tell us what voters want, and the markets price outcomes, not reasons. Both have won. The next step is to dig beneath the surface. When the tables are public and the tools are this good, stopping at the margin is a lazy choice.

Jon Cohen founded TrueDot, an AI-accelerated research company. He was The Washington Post’s polling director from 2006 to 2013 and later was vice president of research at the Pew Research Center and chief research officer at SurveyMonkey.

A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit in Alaska that sought to block certification if the second Dan Sullivan running for Senate causes voter confusion and leads Democrats to flip the seat.

U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ruled the administration hadn’t shown how she could rectify their concerns, as ballots are already prepared and Election Day is on Tuesday.

“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” Gleason wrote.

That Dan Sullivan is listed on Alaska’s ballot alongside incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.

The Alaska Supreme Court has signed off on the new Dan Sullivan’s candidacy, but the Justice Department launched a federal lawsuit last month. The suit asked Gleason to segregate ballots cast for him and block certification of any result impacted by voter confusion until she can conduct an investigation.

The administration can now try to appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9 th Circuit.

The Trump administration has accused Democrats of misleading the judge after a New York Times report emerged that operatives aligned with Peltola had recruited the second Dan Sullivan. Investigations have been launched , but Peltola has denied any personal knowledge of the plan.

Gleason, an appointee of former President Obama who serves on the federal bench in Anchorage, didn’t address the story in her 20-page opinion. Still, she sided with Democrats, Peltola’s campaign and Alaska’s GOP-led government , which all urged her to immediately toss the case.

“Clearly, if this Court were to order that certain ballots will be segregated and subject to a future and as yet unspecified investigation by law enforcement, it would likely result in voter ‘confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls,’” Gleason wrote. “Such late-breaking changes to the election rules are strongly disfavored.”

The Hill has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

articles.title: Will Democrats block the stock trading ban again after the midterm elections?
articles.summary: Senate Democrats voted against a bill that would have banned Congress stock trading. A new poll shows political corruption is voters' top concern.
articles.body: Americans do not agree on much these days, but they certainly agree on this: Members of Congress should not get rich trading stocks while writing the very laws that move those stocks. The failure to ban insider trading in Congress is part of a broader rot now engulfing the swamp. Political corruption, in general, has become a top concern for voters — and for good reason. A new CNBC poll shows, perhaps surprisingly, that it is the most important issue facing the nation: According to CNBC, 36% of voters ranked corruption as the top issue facing the country. To these voters, corruption, and corrupt acts like insider trading, are even more important than the cost of groceries and gas. Despite a slew of arrests in Minnesota, California and New York, where well-connected liberal groups and activists were caught stealing billions in taxpayer dollars, Democrats hold a four-point edge, 35% to 31%, on which party would better handle political corruption. Of those surveyed by CNBC, 93% said members of Congress and the president should not own or trade stock in companies that hold federal contracts, and 89% said companies owned by a sitting president’s immediate family should not receive federal contracts at all. DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID That all seems reasonable enough. But apparently, it isn’t reasonable for Democrats. On Sept. 30, Senate Democrats rejected the Stop Insider Trading Act after it had already passed the House with Democratic votes. If it had passed, the law would have barred members of Congress, their spouses and their dependent children from buying new stock in public companies while in office. It would have also forced public notice before lawmakers could sell what they already hold. CARVILLE TELLS DEMOCRATS TO 'JUST QUIT FIGHTING' AGAINST VOTER ID REQUIREMENTS, WARNS IT POLLS AT 75% But every single Democrat in the Senate voted no. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s, D-N.Y., excuse? He claimed Republicans set the bill up to fail, loading it with intentional "poison pills" so that it would never pass. He also called it toothless, and said it didn’t go far enough. Democrats pointed to a provision requiring voters to show identification at the polls, which an overwhelming majority of Americans support and virtually every other first-world country requires. DEMS HAND GOP FRESH MIDTERM WEAPON BY OPPOSING WIDELY USED VOTER ID Schumer’s other objection — that the bill doesn’t go far enough — is hard to square with his record. One does not refuse to lock his front door because he would prefer an elaborate home security system. A partial reform on the books beats a perfect one that lives only in tailored press releases. Even more to the point: Democrats ran the Senate for years and never delivered the "real" ban on insider trading they now disingenuously purport to want. Senate Democrats’ recent vote against the Stop Insider Trading Act also puts attention back on Nancy Pelosi’s household, which sold 2,000 shares of Visa, worth between $500,000 and $1 million, on July 1, 2024. Less than three months later, the Biden Justice Department filed an antitrust lawsuit against Visa. The stock promptly dropped. As attorney and longtime Trump advisor Michael Caputo recently put it, "Plenty of legal analysts have questioned the suit... whatever the lawsuit ultimately accomplishes, its most conspicuous result so far has been helping a well-connected investor avoid the losses other Visa shareholders suffered." That well-connected investor, of course, is "Princess Nancy" herself. However, the Visa sale wasn’t the first time hubby Paul Pelosi’s stock trading timing attracted scrutiny. In 2022, he bought more than $1 million in Nvidia call options weeks before Congress voted on major subsidies for the chip industry. He then sold them once the story broke. What funny timing! The more things change, the more they stay the same. At the turn of the 20th century, this was sometimes referred to in the jargon of the day as "honest graft." In New York, insiders like George Washington Plunkitt, who ran New York’s infamous political machine of Tammany Hall, declared, "There's an honest graft, and I'm an example of how it works. I might sum up the whole thing by saying: ‘I’ve seen my opportunities and I took ‘em.’" Today, Pelosi’s corruption is so obvious that stock-trading platforms like PelosiTracker, Quiver Quantitative and Unusual Whales attempt to mimic her stock portfolio. In 2024, that portfolio returned more than double the S&P 500. EX-HOUSE DEM WHO RIPPED CONGRESSIONAL STOCK TRADING BAN AS 'BULLS---' CHANGES HER TUNE IN COMEBACK BID The American people are not asking for much. They want the people who write the rules to stop playing the very game those rules govern. Republicans put a bill on the floor that would do that. Senate Democrats killed it. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Senate is out until after the election. When Congress returns for the lame-duck session, it should take the bill up again before the end of the year. Senate Democrats can redeem themselves then — at least on this score.

articles.title: Connecticut Dem Sen Chris Murphy hospitalized for stroke
articles.summary: Connecticut Dem Sen Chris Murphy hospitalized for stroke
articles.body: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized after experiencing a stroke, his chief of staff Allison Herwitt said in a statement released Sunday. Murphy, who is not running in the midterms but has been stumping for Democrats, began feeling numbness in his arm Saturday afternoon while at his son’s hockey game and was taken to a local hospital before being transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring, according to Allison Herwitt. "He is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Herwitt said, adding that Murphy is responding well to treatment and doctors are encouraged by his progress. articles.title: Cong celebrated MLC poll win amid drought, says Bawankule
articles.summary: Revenue minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule alleges Congress used “mutton parties” and bogus voting in Nagpur MLC win; backs voter roll revision to remove duplicates.
articles.body: Nagpur: Revenue minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule on Sunday alleged that Congress lured voters for Nagpur Graduates Constituency polls through “mutton parties” and later celebrated its win lavishly even as “farmers are facing drought”.The minister questioned how Congress can spend on unnecessary things while seeking additional help for farmers. “They talk about drought relief and throw mutton parties. After they won the seat, their celebrations were over-the-top. Congress members could have gone home quietly after victory became official,” said Bawankule.He also said Congress winning the MLC seat is not a big deal. “They have merely retained the seat. It would have assumed significance had they wrested the seat, like in 2020,” he said.The revenue minister added that Congress was always a second choice, but won on a technicality. “BJP came first on first-preference votes. Congress won by taking second-preference votes. All the anti-BJP candidates on the ballot paper gave their second preference to Congress. Still, we have to accept the result and move on,” he said.Dismissing the charge that a weak candidate cost BJP the seat, Bawankule defended Sudhakar Kohale, a former city BJP president and two-time MLA. “Looking at the number of votes he got. If Kohale was the wrong candidate, how did 64,000 voted for him?” he asked.Justifying Special Intensive Revision (SIR) across the country, Bawankule linked the low turnout to bloated rolls. “In Nagpur alone, there are 2 lakh to 2.5 lakh duplicate names and as many dead voters. Why do only 60% vote and not 100%? Names have been added to the list since 2002, but none have been deleted,” he said.Citing the example of Kamptee assembly constituency represented by him, the minister said voters have names in Kamptee, in Hudkeshwar and also in Jaiprakash Nagar. “People vote in a nagar panchayat and then come and vote in the municipal corporation.
